title: WorldClim
text:
What it is
WorldClim provides global gridded climate, such as monthly mean temperature, at resolutions down to 30 arc-seconds (about 1 km). This page uses it mainly to show how the R package geodata reaches such layers: geodata serves per-country tiles of WorldClim 2.1 from geodata.ucdavis.edu, and it identifies Kosovo by the ISO3-style code XKO (ISO2 XK), the same code as GADM, which the GBIF download also filters on.

Kosovo coverage check



How geodata names Kosovo


NAME
ISO3

NAME_LOCAL




Kosovo
XKO
XK
Kosova





The country tile covers 19.5–22.0° E and 41.5–43.5° N, wider than Kosovo. Inside the outline: 17,215 cells, 0 no-data; annual mean of the monthly means 0.1 to 12.7 °C (mean 9.1 °C).
The tile is cut to a rectangle around Kosovo, not to its border: geodata leaves the clipping to the user, which is why the outline from the pipeline is applied here.
The code matters more than it looks. geodata finds Kosovo because it uses GADM’s list of countries, where Kosovo is XKO. Both wrong guesses were tried while writing this page. Asking for “XKX”, the code the pipeline stamps on its own records, stops with “unknown country: XKX”. Asking for “SRB”, in the hope of catching Kosovo inside Serbia, returns Serbia’s tile, a rectangle from 42° to 46.5° N that takes in most of Kosovo by accident and stops short of its southern mountains. The same lookup, geodata::country_codes(), is worth running before any per-country download from this package, and its answer recorded, as the table above does. geodata also caches what it downloads under the path it is given, so a second render reads the local file rather than the server; here that cache sits under data/sources/worldclim/.

The same kind of covariates as CHELSA, with the advantage that geodata makes them one line of code, which suits teaching. Two climatologies from different methods also give a cheap check on each other in Kosovo’s mountains. National screening only (tier).

The country tile is a rectangle; clip it before computing national figures.

title: EU for Natura 2000 in Serbia
text:
What it is
“EU for Natura 2000 in Serbia” was an EU-funded technical-assistance project that ended on 30 November 2021. Serbia’s Natura 2000 portal, run for the Ministry of Environmental Protection, reports that in about two and a half years a team of national and international experts identified 277 potential Sites of Community Interest (pSCIs) and 85 Special Protection Areas (SPAs) under the Habitats and Birds Directives. The Ministry, the Institute for Nature Conservation of Serbia, the Institute for Nature Conservation of Vojvodina Province and the Serbian Environmental Protection Agency took part.
The project’s own site describes its purpose as establishing the first list of potential Natura 2000 sites, “together with the development of an information system, database and GIS”. The list itself, its boundaries and its forms are not published on either site.

title: EU for Natura 2000 in Serbia
text:
Kosovo coverage check






WarningTo be completed



The draft site boundaries are not published, so no overlay with Kosovo’s border could be run. The pages opened say nothing about sites in or next to Kosovo. Once the boundaries are obtained: list every pSCI and SPA within 20 km of the border, measure how much of each lies inside Kosovo, and record the country code on each site. Serbia’s candidate Emerald sites already extend into Kosovo under code RS (see Emerald Network), so the same must be checked for the Natura 2000 list.

title: EU for Natura 2000 in Serbia
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
Sites on Šar, Prokletije and Kopaonik stop at a border the species do not recognise. A Kosovo proposal that ends where a Serbian or Macedonian one begins, with the same habitat on both sides, is easier to defend in the biogeographical process than one drawn without looking across. The Serbian list would also show which features a neighbour with a comparable fauna and flora judged to need sites, which is a check on Kosovo’s own sufficiency ledger. The tier depends on the boundary scale, which is not yet known.

title: EU for Natura 2000 in Serbia
text:
Caveats and sensitivity

A potential site list is a technical proposal, not a designation, and may change before Serbia submits it.
Only the project’s summary numbers were verified; nothing about individual sites was.
Any site list that includes Kosovo’s territory under Serbian codes needs to be read as a data question, not a statement on status.

Until then there is nothing to integrate. pipeline.R is not changed.

title: Red Book of Vascular Flora of the Republic of Kosovo
text:
What it is
The Red Book of Vascular Flora of the Republic of Kosovo was prepared by a team led by Fadil Millaku (editor-in-chief) with Ferat Rexhepi, Elez Krasniqi, Qazim Pajazitaj, Xhavit Mala and Naim Berisha, published by the Ministry of Environment and Spatial Planning in 2013 with support from German development cooperation (GIZ). Its English summary states that 237 taxa were assessed against the IUCN criteria: 1 Extinct, 1 Extinct in the Wild, 61 Critically Endangered, 86 Endangered, 19 Vulnerable, 34 Near Threatened and 35 Least Concern. The selection drew on the literature, on Administrative Instruction No. 18/2012 on protected species, and on the state of each species in the field.
The methods are worth noting for what they imply about data. For every species assessed, the team took herbarium samples, photographs and GPS coordinates, counted mature individuals where possible, and measured area of occupancy and extent of occurrence on the UTM grid. The locality data therefore exist, but they are not in the summary.

That needs the species list from the full book. title: Red Book of Vascular Flora of the Republic of Kosovo
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
The report already flags species on the EU annexes and on the global Red List. Neither captures what is threatened in Kosovo itself. A national list of 148 Critically Endangered or Endangered plants would let the report mark records of nationally threatened species, and let site selection favour candidate sites that hold them. The field coordinates behind the assessments would, if shared, be among the most precise plant data for the country. The list serves the national tier.

title: Red Book of Vascular Flora of the Republic of Kosovo
text:
Caveats and sensitivity

The summary alone gives counts, not species.
National categories apply regional IUCN guidelines and cannot be compared one-to-one with global ones.
Several of the Critically Endangered taxa are small populations of endemics; their coordinates must never be published precisely.

title: Red Book of Vascular Flora of the Republic of Kosovo
text:
Integration into the pipeline
Medium effort once a table exists: a proposed R/build_red_list.R, modelled on R/build_directive_list.R, would resolve the names and write data/kosovo_red_list_flora.csv; pipeline.R would then add a national category column to every plant record. pipeline.R is not changed here.

              error = function(e) NULL)
if (!is.null(g)) {
  print(sf::st_drop_geometry(g[g$CNTR_ID %in% c("XK", "RS"), c("CNTR_ID", "ISO3_CODE", "NAME_ENGL")]))

    CNTR_ID ISO3_CODE NAME_ENGL
142      RS       SRB    Serbia
    xmin     ymin     xmax     ymax 
18.87271 41.86428 23.00621 46.18793 


GISCO’s 2024 country layer has no feature for Kosovo, and Serbia’s polygon reaches south to about 41.86° N: Kosovo is inside it. The pipeline already knows this (R/functions.R compares its border against GISCO’s international boundary only), but anyone who clips data to “Serbia” from GISCO is clipping Kosovo in with it.
Across this section, Kosovo turned up under at least six different identifiers: XK (GBIF, EU country code), XKO (GADM, geodata), XKX (the pipeline’s own ISO3-style code), KS (EFFIS), RS (Emerald candidate sites, BirdLife’s inventory and GISCO, where it is merged into Serbia), and Ko (Euro+Med). A script that filters any of these sources by one code will silently miss what the others file under another.

title: National park spatial plans
text:
What it is
Kosovo’s two national parks, Bjeshkët e Nemuna in the west and Sharri in the south, are the core of any future Natura 2000 network. Each is governed by a spatial plan that zones the park and says where development may go.
The Plani Hapësinor për Parkun Kombëtar “Bjeshkët e Nemuna” is published by the Ministry of Environment, Spatial Planning and Infrastructure and drafted by its Institute for Spatial Planning; the PDF (89 pages, in Albanian) dates from June 2023. It notes that the park law adopted by the Assembly on 13 December 2012 gave an area of 62,488 ha, revised to 63,028 ha after detailed measurement, and it defines an impact zone of 50 m around the park boundary.
For Sharri the document found is a draft Strategic Environmental Assessment of the park’s spatial plan (161 pages, PDF dated March 2025), prepared with UN-Habitat. It sets environmental objectives for the plan, among them avoiding the fragmentation of habitats and impacts on the integrity of “protected areas and Natura 2000 areas”.

title: Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan 2016–2020
text:
What it is
The Ministry of Environment and Spatial Planning’s Action Plan for Biodiversity 2016–2020 revises the implementation part of Kosovo’s Strategy and Action Plan for Biodiversity 2011–2020, which the Assembly approved on 7 October 2011. The English PDF runs to 78 pages. It is interesting less for its measures than for its candour about the starting point. Among the main problems it lists are the lack of full inventories for flora, fauna and habitats (except the Red Book of Vascular Flora), the lack of a red list of fauna, and the lack of national biodiversity indicators.
On Natura 2000 it records three facts that other pages in this section depend on. Kosovo “is not a Party to the Bern Convention”, so no Emerald network was developed. A report of preliminary Natura 2000 sites was drafted in 2008 under the Sustainable Forest Management project. And an administrative instruction of 2013 on a national ecological network put the Kosovo Institute for Nature Protection in charge of establishing it.

title: Natural history collections holding Kosovo material
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
Historical specimens are the baseline against which losses are judged, and for many invertebrates and plants they are the only evidence of occurrence. For a sufficiency ledger (question 4) an old specimen from a site is a reason to survey it, not proof that the species is still there. Most old labels give a place name only, so the data serve the national tier.

Caveats and sensitivity

Only GBIF was checked. Material held but not published is by definition invisible here.
Specimen localities of rare plants and insects are sensitive; publishing them precisely can prompt collecting.

title: Kosovo National Forest Inventory 2012
text:
What it is
Kosovo’s second National Forest Inventory (NFI) was carried out in 2012. The public abstract, hosted by the Norwegian Forestry Group, says that “for the first time, Kosovo’s entire forest area has been assessed”. Of 3,453 permanent sample plots laid across the country, 1,860 forest plots were visited in six months of 2012 by twelve foresters, re-measuring trees mapped in the first inventory of 2003. The abstract reports 481,000 ha of forest, 45 per cent of the land, with a growing stock of about 40 million m³ that has stayed stable since 2003. It also records that almost 99 per cent of forests show traces of human activity, that fire affected over 12,000 ha, and that the two national parks hold about 90 per cent of the coniferous growing stock.

section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo

What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
Forest is almost half of Kosovo, and forest habitat types will be a large part of any Natura 2000 network. Plot data would ground-truth the land-cover screens, give a first estimate of the area of forest types, and provide structure and dead-wood indicators for the “structure and functions” parameter of habitat assessment. The KEPA table carries 217 distinct codes and NatDA 256. Taken literally, only 22 codes appear in both, because the two lists abbreviate the categories differently: strict reserves are RN in the table and NR in NatDA, national parks PK and NP, protected landscapes PM and PL. Translating the table’s prefixes to NatDA’s (and trying both MN and NM for natural monuments) matches 201 of the table’s 217 codes. Still unmatched in the table: MM_102, MN_009, MN_056, MN_057, MN_058, MN_070, MN_075, MN_079, MN_081, NN_082, NN_101, PN_001, RN_001, RN_002, RN_010, ZVM_001.
A code with no counterpart is not necessarily an error: text extraction from a PDF table can split or merge cells, and NatDA may hold sites designated after 2020. But the prefix mismatch itself is a finding. A join on the site code between the national table and the EEA reporting fails silently for all but a few natural monuments, so any tool that links them must translate the prefixes first, and the translation above is an inference to be confirmed by KEPA.

section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
A Natura 2000 proposal starts from the existing national sites, and the report’s figures on how much is protected rest on NatDA. If the national table and NatDA disagree, the report’s coverage figures inherit the disagreement. The table also carries the IUCN category and short descriptions of each site’s values, a useful first pointer to what each site was protected for. It serves the national tier; boundaries come from NatDA.

title: Table of protected areas in Kosovo, 2020
text:
Caveats and sensitivity

Codes were extracted automatically from a PDF, and the extraction is only as good as the PDF’s text layer.
The table has no boundaries; any area comparison must use NatDA.
No sensitive content.

title: Table of protected areas in Kosovo, 2020
text:
Integration into the pipeline
Low effort. The codes already match NatDA’s national_id, so a proposed check_register_against_natda(table_codes, protected_areas) could run after kosovo_protected_areas() in pipeline.R and report mismatches in the run log. A machine-readable table from KEPA would make the PDF step unnecessary. pipeline.R is not changed here.

title: Data sources
text:
The report is built on one GBIF download, cleaned against an OpenStreetMap outline, and set against the EEA’s register of Kosovo’s protected areas, the EU annex lists, the global Red List and the Union list of invasive species. This section looks beyond them. Each page below takes one candidate dataset from a desk review of what else could inform Natura 2000 site identification in Kosovo*, checks what its custodian actually publishes, and, where the data could be reached, runs a check against Kosovo’s territory. The pages are written so that each can be read, re-run and completed on its own.
The rule throughout is that a value is shown only if it was verified. Every filled field in the registry has a row in sources/registry_evidence.csv naming the page it was checked against and the date; a field without one is blanked automatically and appears as “— to be completed”. A gap is not an error; a guess would be. The precision tiers named below (national screening, site-level delineation, Standard Data Form) are those defined on the Natura 2000 page.

The 47 datasets stand as follows: Complete: 9; Partial: 19; Documented only: 12; Awaiting request: 4; Lead, not verified: 3; Not applicable to Kosovo: 0. Across all of them, 60 per cent of the verifiable registry fields are filled.

title: Data sources
text:
What the checks found
Four findings cut across the pages and are worth knowing before reading any one of them.

Kosovo hides under other codes. The same territory appears as XK (GBIF), XKO (GADM and geodata), KS (EFFIS) and Ko (Euro+Med), and inside RS where European data were compiled with Serbia: Serbia’s candidate Emerald sites cover about a fifth of Kosovo, BirdLife holds Kosovo’s IBAs in its Serbia inventory, GISCO has no Kosovo feature at all, and EFFIS files some Kosovo fires under RS. Any query by a single country code undercounts.
The EU’s own reporting stops about 50 km away. Kosovo’s four neighbours are outside the EU, so the nearest Article 17 and Article 12 cells are in Bulgaria.
European habitat models do cover Kosovo. The EUNIS level-3 maps and the ecosystem-type map have no gaps inside the outline, which makes them the closest thing to the Annex I map Kosovo lacks.
Much of what Kosovo knows is in PDFs. The red books, the protected-area table and the park plans are published, but not as data; and the national protected-area table and the EEA register use different code prefixes, so they cannot be joined without translation.

title: Data sources
text:
Data gaps
Some of what a Natura 2000 proposal needs does not exist in any of the sources above. Each gap is stated with why it matters for the Standard Data Form (SDF) and who could close it.

1. No Annex I habitat map or inventory
Missing: a map of Annex I habitat types for Kosovo. The EUNIS model and the report’s CORINE screen say where to look, not what is there. For the SDF: section 3.1 needs each habitat’s cover, representativity and conservation, which only mapped polygons provide (question 3). Who: the Kosovo Institute for Nature Protection with University of Prishtina botanists, by field mapping at 1:10,000, starting in the pilot sites.


2. No official or draft Natura 2000 or Emerald site list with boundaries
Missing: any candidate site list for Kosovo. The 2008 identification (Mustafa) is known only from citations, and Kosovo is not a Bern Convention Party, so it has no Emerald list of its own. For the SDF: there is nothing yet to fill one for. Who: the Ministry and KINP, which the NBSAP makes responsible for the ecological network.


3. No confirmed IBA or KBA boundaries
Missing: the digital boundaries of the four IBAs that concern Kosovo; only centroids are public. For the SDF: SPA proposals start from the IBA inventory, and how much of each IBA lies in Kosovo is unknown. Who: a request to the World Database of KBAs, whose terms come with the request form.


4. No published national species monitoring data
Missing: surveillance data with method and effort. The red books of fauna and flora assess species but do not release their localities as data. For the SDF: section 3.2’s population and data-quality fields need surveyed records, not casual ones. Who: KEPA and KINP, with the red-book authors; a data-use agreement could release localities at a generalised resolution.


5. No population-size data for SDF section 3.2
Missing: population estimates with units (pairs, individuals, localities) for Annex II species and Annex I birds. The IBA factsheets give a few, several from 2008–2013 or earlier. For the SDF: section 3.2 requires minimum and maximum population with a unit and a data-quality code. Who: standardised counts in the pilot sites (question 6); the eBird Basic Dataset for effort-based bird data.


6. No wetland, peatland, cave or grassland inventories
Missing: national inventories of the habitat groups most likely to hold priority Annex I types: wetlands and mires, caves, dry and mountain grasslands. For the SDF: these are small or scattered habitats that land-cover data miss at a 25 ha minimum unit. Who: KINP with specialists; the natural monuments in the national table, many of them springs and caves, are a starting list.


7. No Article 17-style range assessments, and no delineation of biogeographical regions within Kosovo
Missing: national range and distribution maps on the 10 km grid, as EU countries report under Article 17, and a Kosovo delineation of the biogeographical regions finer than the European 1:1,000,000 line. For the SDF: a site’s contribution is judged against the national population and range in its region. Who: KINP, as the NBSAP foresees; the European layer is the starting point.


8. Scattered evidence for Annex II invertebrates and freshwater fish
Missing: systematic data for the Annex II groups least covered by casual recording. The data papers add caddisflies and plants but no Annex II list; the taxon atlases are unverified. For the SDF: without them, sites cannot be proposed for these species at all. Who: university specialists, with targeted surveys in the rivers the hydropower inventory shows under pressure.

title: Data sources
text:
How this section is maintained

sources/registry.csv holds one row per dataset; sources/registry_evidence.csv one row per verified value. Edit both together.
R/sources_helpers.R reads them, blanks unverified values, and draws the tables, badges and checklists.
Pages cache what they download under data/sources/<slug>/. Small open extracts are committed; PDFs and anything over 50 MB are not.
This folder renders with freeze: auto. After editing the registry or the helpers, run quarto render sources/ so every page picks up the change.

The Independent Commission for Mines and Minerals (ICMM, KPMM in Albanian) is Kosovo’s mining regulator. title: Independent Commission for Mines and Minerals: licences and GIS
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
Mining is a pressure that a site proposal must face early, because a licence granted inside a candidate site constrains its designation and management. Knowing where exploration and mining licences lie, and how they overlap the existing protected areas and the habitat screen, is part of the pressure analysis for an SDF (section 4.3, threats and pressures) and for any appropriate assessment. Licence polygons would serve the site tier.

A login is required; the terms of access are unknown.
Licence areas are not mine footprints; they mark where activity is permitted.

title: HydroSHEDS
text:
What it is
HydroSHEDS is a suite of global hydrographic data derived from elevation data: flow directions, catchments (HydroBASINS) and rivers (HydroRIVERS). HydroRIVERS represents all rivers of the world as a vector network extracted from the HydroSHEDS grids at 15 arc-seconds, about 500 m, with attributes such as flow order and discharge. It is “freely available for scientific, educational and commercial use” under the HydroSHEDS licence, with attribution. Where EU-Hydro is a photo-interpreted European network at 1:50,000, HydroRIVERS is coarser and modelled, but identical in method everywhere, including across all of Kosovo’s borders.

The Europe file is a 68 MB zipped shapefile. A shapefile has no spatial index GDAL can use over HTTP, so it is downloaded once, outside version control, and only the Kosovo extract is kept. The contrast with the GeoPackages read remotely on other pages (Article 17, the protected areas in the pipeline) is the teaching point: a format with an R-tree index can be queried in place, one without must be fetched whole. The archive’s size, checksum and date are recorded below, since it is not committed.


Show the download and cut
build_error <- NULL
if (!file.exists(cache)) {
  build_error <- tryCatch({
    if (!file.exists(zip)) {
      got <- try_access(url, zip, timeout = 900)
      if (!got$success) stop(got$error %||% paste("HTTP", got$http_code))
    }
    shp <- grep("\\.shp$", unzip(zip, list = TRUE)$Name, value = TRUE)
    ko  <- st_union(kosovo_outline())
    box <- st_as_text(st_as_sfc(st_bbox(ko)))
    r   <- st_read(paste0("/vsizip/", zip, "/", shp), wkt_filter = box, quiet = TRUE)
    r   <- suppressWarnings(st_intersection(st_make_valid(r), ko))
    st_write(r, cache, delete_dsn = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)
    NULL
  }, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
}
have_cache <- file.exists(cache)

The desk review grouped five kinds of European distribution atlas under one lead, and confirmed no URL for any of them. Nothing on this page has yet been verified. text:
What it is
Euro+Med PlantBase is the checklist of the vascular plants of Europe and the Mediterranean, recording for each accepted taxon the areas in which it occurs. What it is
EU-Hydro is the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service’s photo-interpreted river network for the EEA38 countries and the United Kingdom: river lines ordered by Strahler number, inland water polygons, and a drainage model derived from the EU-DEM. Its metadata contain a sentence that bears directly on Kosovo: for Türkiye, Albania, Bosnia-Herzegovina, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Kosovo and Serbia, “no spatial data for any category of water bodies was available”. build_error <- NULL
if (!file.exists(cache)) {
  build_error <- tryCatch({
    source("../R/functions.R", local = TRUE)
    ko <- st_transform(st_union(kosovo_outline()), 3035)
    bb <- st_bbox(st_transform(ko, 4326))
    rivers <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(strahler_layers), function(o) {
      # A layer with nothing in the box, or nothing left after clipping, is
      # skipped rather than allowed to stop the build.
      x <- tryCatch(arcgis_query_sf(paste0(svc, "/", strahler_layers[[o]]), bb,
                                    fields = "OBJECTID", verbose = FALSE),
                    error = function(e) NULL)
      if (is.null(x)) return(NULL)
      x <- suppressWarnings(st_intersection(st_make_valid(x), ko))
      x <- suppressWarnings(st_collection_extract(x, "LINESTRING"))
      if (!nrow(x)) return(NULL)
      st_sf(strahler = rep(as.integer(o), nrow(x)), geometry = st_geometry(x))
    }))
    water <- arcgis_query_sf(paste0(svc, "/2"), bb, fields = "OBJECTID", verbose = FALSE)
    water <- suppressWarnings(st_intersection(st_make_valid(water), ko))
    st_write(rivers, cache, layer = "rivers", delete_dsn = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)
    st_write(st_sf(geometry = st_geometry(water)), cache, layer = "inland_water",
             append = FALSE, quiet = TRUE)
    NULL
  }, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
}

title: EU-Hydro
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo

What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
Freshwater habitats (3260 water courses, 91E0 alluvial forests, 92A0 willow and poplar galleries) and Annex II fish follow the river network, and a Strahler order separates headwater streams from the main rivers. River lines are also natural site boundaries. EU-Hydro is one network for all the EEA’s member and cooperating countries, which makes it a natural choice for a Kosovo network meant to join its neighbours’. At 1:50,000 it serves the national tier and outlines for sites.

    if (is.null(r) || !r$count) return(data.frame(query = x, title = NA, publisher = NA))
    data.frame(query = x, title = r$results$title,
               publisher = r$results$publishingOrganizationTitle)
  }))
  write.csv(hits, cache, row.names = FALSE)
}

title: EFFIS burnt areas
text:
What it is
The European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS), part of the Copernicus emergency services, maps burnt areas across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa from MODIS and VIIRS satellite imagery. Each mapped fire comes with its dates, its area, and the share of it that was broadleaved, coniferous or mixed forest, scrub, agricultural or other land, and the share inside Natura 2000. EFFIS distributes the data through web map and web feature services, as downloads, and through a request form for historical extracts.

The web map service lists yearly layers of burnt areas (modis.ba.poly.2016 to modis.ba.poly.2025 among them). The web feature service’s capabilities request timed out, but a direct GetFeature request for a box around Kosovo returned every burnt area in it as GML, which the build step below uses.


Show the WFS request
build_error <- NULL
if (!file.exists(cache)) {
  build_error <- tryCatch({
    ko <- st_union(kosovo_outline())
    bb <- st_bbox(st_transform(ko, 3857))
    # EPSG:3857 keeps x before y; with EPSG:4326, WFS 1.1 swaps the axes.
    url <- sprintf(paste0(wfs, "?service=WFS&version=1.1.0&request=GetFeature",
                          "&typename=ms:modis.ba.poly&srsName=EPSG:3857",
                          "&bbox=%f,%f,%f,%f,EPSG:3857&maxFeatures=50000"),
                   bb[1], bb[2], bb[3], bb[4])
    gml <- tempfile(fileext = ".gml")
    got <- try_access(url, gml, timeout = 300)
    if (!got$success) stop(got$error %||% paste("HTTP", got$http_code))
    x <- st_read(gml, quiet = TRUE) |> st_transform(3035) |> st_make_valid()
    x <- x[, setdiff(names(x), "msGeometry")]
    # Keep only the part of each fire inside Kosovo, as polygons: a fire that
    # merely touches the border leaves lines or points, which carry no area.
    x <- suppressWarnings(st_intersection(x, st_transform(ko, 3035)))
    x <- suppressWarnings(st_collection_extract(x, "POLYGON"))
    # Extraction can split one fire into several rows; put each back together.
    parts <- split(seq_len(nrow(x)), x$id)
    geom  <- do.call(c, lapply(parts, function(i) st_union(st_geometry(x)[i])))
    attrs <- st_drop_geometry(x)[!duplicated(x$id), ]
    attrs <- attrs[match(names(parts), as.character(attrs$id)), ]
    x <- st_sf(attrs, geometry = st_cast(geom, "MULTIPOLYGON"))
    x$in_kosovo_ha <- as.numeric(st_area(x)) / 1e4
    x <- x[x$in_kosovo_ha > 0, ]
    x$year <- as.integer(substr(x$FIREDATE, 1, 4))
    # Areas are measured above, on the full geometry; the stored outlines are
    # generalised to 25 m, well below MODIS's own resolution, to keep the
    # cache small.
    x <- st_simplify(x, dTolerance = 25, preserveTopology = TRUE)
    st_write(x[, c("id", "FIREDATE", "FINALDATE", "LASTUPDATE", "COUNTRY", "AREA_HA",
                   "BROADLEA", "CONIFER", "MIXED", "SCLEROPH", "TRANSIT", "OTHERNATLC",
                   "AGRIAREAS", "ARTIFSURF", "OTHERLC", "year", "in_kosovo_ha")],
             cache, delete_dsn = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)
    NULL
  }, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
}
have_cache <- file.exists(cache)

title: EFFIS burnt areas
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
Fire is a recurrent pressure on Kosovo’s forests and grasslands; the NFI 2012 abstract counts over 12,000 ha affected. EFFIS gives a consistent, dated record of where it happened, and how much of each fire was forest, which is what an SDF’s pressure section and a habitat’s “future prospects” need. It also shows which fires burnt inside existing protected areas. At the scale of MODIS mapping it serves the national tier, with the larger fires usable at site level.

title: EFFIS burnt areas
text:
Caveats and sensitivity

Small fires fall below the satellite’s mapping threshold and are missing.
Perimeters are mapped from imagery at a coarse resolution, not surveyed.
No species locations; nothing sensitive.

title: EFFIS burnt areas
text:
Integration into the pipeline
Low effort. A proposed effis_burnt_areas(boundary) in R/functions.R would run the request above and write data/kosovo_burnt_areas.gpkg; the report’s protected-area section could then add burnt hectares per site. pipeline.R is not changed.

title: Biogeographical regions of Europe
text:
What it is
The biogeographical regions dataset is, in the words of its catalogue record, “the official delineations used in the Habitats Directive” and for the Emerald Network under the Bern Convention. The 2016 version (edition 01.00, 26 January 2016) corrected the Pannonian region of Serbia, among other fixes. The desk review listed it as a lead. It is in fact already in use: the pipeline reads it from the EEA’s map service, clips it to Kosovo in kosovo_biogeo_regions(), caches it as data/kosovo_biogeo_regions.gpkg, and uses it in the habitat screen, so that the crosswalk can differ between regions.

title: Biogeographical regions of Europe
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
Every Natura 2000 site is assessed in its biogeographical region, and sufficiency is judged region by region. Which region each part of Kosovo lies in therefore decides which biogeographical seminar would review its sites and which reference lists apply. The NBSAP names a clear delineation of these boundaries within Kosovo as a preparatory task; this dataset is the European starting point for it. It serves the national tier.

Drawn at 1:1,000,000 or coarser: the boundary is good to about a kilometre at best, as R/functions.R notes.
No sensitive content.

title: eBird and Observation.org records outside GBIF
text:
What it is
eBird, run by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, and Observation.org are the two citizen-science platforms that contribute most to Kosovo’s GBIF record. Both publish to GBIF: eBird as the “EOD – eBird Observation Dataset” under CC BY 4.0, Observation.org as “Observation.org, Nature data from around the World” under CC BY-NC 4.0. Both are already among the datasets in the report’s download, and eBird alone supplies nine in ten of its bird records.
The desk review asked about records not in GBIF. For eBird that means the eBird Basic Dataset (EBD). The site’s Natura 2000 page describes it as carrying what the GBIF copy leaves out: the effort fields and the flag that says a checklist reports every species detected, which turn a list of sightings into a survey with non-detections. eBird’s own description could not be read to confirm this (see Access). For Observation.org it means records the platform does not pass to GBIF.

title: eBird and Observation.org records outside GBIF
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
An SPA case needs counts with effort, not scattered presences (question 6). The EBD’s effort fields and complete-checklist flag are what make eBird usable for that: they allow detection rates, seasonal occupancy and absences to be computed for Ligatina e Hencit/Radevës and the other bird sites. Stationary counts with precise locations can reach the delineation tier; travelling checklists stay at screening.

title: eBird and Observation.org records outside GBIF
text:
Caveats and sensitivity

The EBD terms could not be read; the licence of the full eBird database is therefore not recorded.
Both platforms hide or generalise sensitive species in their public data; what applies to Kosovo is unknown.
Observation.org’s GBIF copy is CC BY-NC, which limits commercial reuse of anything derived from it.

title: eBird and Observation.org records outside GBIF
text:
Integration into the pipeline
Medium effort for the EBD: a proposed read_ebd(path, boundary) using the auk package would filter the file to Kosovo and keep checklist-level effort beside the GBIF records, linked by checklist identifier rather than merged. pipeline.R is not changed.

title: Copernicus land monitoring: CORINE, High Resolution Layers, Riparian Zones
text:
What it is
The Copernicus Land Monitoring Service (CLMS), operated for this part by the European Environment Agency, produces the pan-European land products this page groups together. CORINE Land Cover (CLC) maps land cover every six years at a 25 ha minimum mapping unit, as R/functions.R records. The High Resolution Layers map single themes, such as tree cover and grassland, at a finer resolution. The Riparian Zones product maps land cover along rivers for 2012 and 2018, with a change layer between them.
One of these is already in the report. pipeline.R reads CLC2018 for Kosovo from the EEA’s map service, clips it to the OpenStreetMap outline and uses it for the screen of potential Annex I habitats; its provenance is recorded in clc_sources in R/functions.R. The desk review listed CLC as a lead, so this page records that it is in fact in use.

title: Copernicus land monitoring: CORINE, High Resolution Layers, Riparian Zones
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
CLC is the basis of the report’s national screen for potential Annex I habitats. The High Resolution Layers could sharpen it: a fine-grained grassland layer would separate meadows from arable land far better than a 25 ha polygon, which matters for grassland types such as 6210, 6510 and 6520. Riparian Zones would do the same for alluvial forests and river habitats, 91E0 and 92A0. All serve the national screening tier; the HRLs come closest to the site tier.

title: Copernicus land monitoring: CORINE, High Resolution Layers, Riparian Zones
text:
Caveats and sensitivity

CLC’s 25 ha unit hides small habitats entirely; the report says so where it uses it.
Coverage of the HRLs and Riparian Zones for Kosovo is unconfirmed.
No sensitive content.

Kosovo is fully covered. The values are those GDAL returns after applying the scale and offset stored in each file. No country attribute exists, so no country code applies.
Two things about the read are worth teaching. First, nothing is downloaded in full: GDAL’s /vsicurl/ prefix turns the file’s address into something terra can open, and the crop asks the server only for the parts of the global grid that cover Kosovo. Second, the check counts no-data cells inside the outline rather than trusting a map to look complete. A European or global product can leave a country blank for reasons of its own, and a blank that falls on the country being studied is easy to miss on a map at continental scale. Here there is none.

title: Hydropower projects on Balkan rivers
text:
What it is
Since 2012 RiverWatch and EuroNatur have mapped hydropower plants on Balkan rivers, with data compiled by Fluvius in Vienna. The 2024 update, announced on 14 March 2025, counts 3,188 projects planned, 94 under construction and 1,836 in operation across the region, with 110 new installations since 2022. The 2022 update, prepared by Ulrich Schwarz, lists Kosovo separately: 89 plants planned and 10 under construction at the time, and it names Kosovo among the countries where most new plants came into operation since 2020. It overlays the plants with protected areas, including Emerald and proposed Natura 2000 areas, and was delivered in GIS formats and as the online map at balkanrivers.net.

title: Article 12 reporting under the Birds Directive, 2013–2018
text:
What it is
Article 12 of the Birds Directive asks every EU Member State to report, every six years, on the size, trend and distribution of its bird populations. The EEA publishes the 2013–2018 round as a tabular dataset (population sizes and short- and long-term trends, breeding and wintering) and a spatial dataset of 10 km grid cells in which each country mapped where each species occurs. The public spatial version dates from April 2021 and was published on the EEA datahub on 1 March 2022, under CC-BY 4.0.
The EEA’s README describes the spatial file as gridded distribution data “as reported by EU Member States”, aggregated by species and country, and states that it is the public version without sensitive species.

Show how the border-zone extract is built
build_error <- NULL
if (!file.exists(cache)) {
  build_error <- tryCatch({
    Sys.setenv(GDAL_DISABLE_READDIR_ON_OPEN = "EMPTY_DIR",
               CPL_VSIL_CURL_CHUNK_SIZE = "1048576",
               CPL_VSIL_CURL_CACHE_SIZE = "524288000")
    src  <- paste0("/vsicurl/", share)
    ko   <- st_transform(st_union(kosovo_outline()), 3035)
    zone <- st_buffer(ko, 100000)
    birds <- st_read(src,
      layer = "EU_ART12_birds_distribution_2013_2018_without_sensitive_species",
      wkt_filter = st_as_text(st_as_sfc(st_bbox(zone))), quiet = TRUE)

    # Rebuild the EEA 10 km grid, whose corners sit on round 10 km multiples
    # of EPSG:3035, and test each cell's centre against the dissolved ranges.
    bb <- st_bbox(zone)
    bb[c("xmin", "ymin")] <- floor(bb[c("xmin", "ymin")] / 1e4) * 1e4
    bb[c("xmax", "ymax")] <- ceiling(bb[c("xmax", "ymax")] / 1e4) * 1e4
    grid <- st_sf(geometry = st_make_grid(st_as_sfc(bb), cellsize = 1e4))
    grid <- grid[lengths(st_intersects(grid, zone)) > 0, ]
    xy <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(grid))
    grid$cell_id <- sprintf("10kmE%dN%d", floor(xy[, 1] / 1e4), floor(xy[, 2] / 1e4))
    grid$dist_km <- round(as.numeric(st_distance(grid, ko)) / 1000, 1)

    hit <- st_intersects(st_centroid(st_geometry(grid)), birds)
    a <- st_drop_geometry(birds)
    long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(hit), function(i) {
      if (!length(hit[[i]])) return(NULL)
      f <- a[hit[[i]], ]
      data.frame(cell_id = grid$cell_id[i], code = f$speciescodeEU,
                 name = f$speciesnameEU, season = f$season,
                 country = f$country, trend = f$population_trend)
    }))
    grid <- grid[grid$cell_id %in% long$cell_id, ]
    st_write(grid, cache, layer = "cells", delete_dsn = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)
    st_write(long, cache, layer = "features", append = FALSE, quiet = TRUE)
    NULL
  }, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
}
have_cache <- file.exists(cache)

title: Article 12 reporting under the Birds Directive, 2013–2018
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
The report already has Kosovo’s own bird records from GBIF and the IBA qualifying species on the Natura 2000 page. This file adds the regional frame around them: the Annex I species that the nearest EU countries hold as breeding populations, and their reported trends. A species breeding 60 km away that has no Kosovo record is a survey question; one reported declining there raises the stakes of a Kosovo population. At 10 km the data serve the national screening tier.

title: Article 12 reporting under the Birds Directive, 2013–2018
text:
Caveats and sensitivity

The public version leaves out sensitive species entirely, as the EEA says. Raptors, grouse and other persecuted birds may therefore be absent here although reported to the Commission.
The nearest data lie in Bulgaria, because Kosovo’s four neighbours are not EU members; the Montenegrin, Albanian, Macedonian and Serbian mountains that share Kosovo’s bird fauna are blank.
Near Kosovo the file holds breeding distributions only; no wintering map reaches this far, and passage is never mapped. The lists therefore say nothing about the migrants that give Ligatina e Hencit/Radevës its value.
Annex I is matched by exact name, so a taxon the EEA names differently (for example with “s. str.” or “all others”) is not flagged even when it is listed.

title: Article 12 reporting under the Birds Directive, 2013–2018
text:
Integration into the pipeline
Low effort, and the same function as for Article 17 with a different layer: a proposed art12_border_species(boundary, radius_km = c(50, 100)) in R/functions.R, run beside the IBA step, whose output a report section on the SPA route could read. pipeline.R is not changed by this page.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
text:
Kosovo sits within the Balkan biodiversity hotspot, one of the most species-rich regions in Europe. Evidence-based conservation — designating protected areas, screening development proposals, and reporting against the EU Nature Directives — depends on knowing which species occur where.
The Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) aggregates species occurrence records published by museums, research institutions, monitoring programmes and citizen-science platforms worldwide. This report brings the GBIF holdings for the territory of Kosovo into a single, quality-controlled, openly downloadable evidence base, and highlights the records that relate to species protected under the EU Birds and Habitats Directives or assessed as threatened on the IUCN Red List — and to the invasive alien species the EU regulates as a threat to all of them.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
text:
Data provenance and citation
The occurrence data were obtained through the GBIF asynchronous download service, which mints a permanent Digital Object Identifier (DOI) for the exact extract used here. Citing that DOI allows any reader to retrieve the identical dataset, and passes credit back to the institutions that published the records.

Dataset DOI: https://doi.org/10.15468/dl.wzpexq GBIF download key: 0003504-260903145123482 Retrieved: 29 September 2026 Spatial filter: GADM boundary XKO (Kosovo) Contributing datasets: 125, from 80 publishing institutions Suggested citation GBIF Occurrence Download https://doi.org/10.15468/dl.wzpexq Accessed from R via rgbif (https://github.com/ropensci/rgbif) on 2026-09-05

Two reference layers are used alongside the occurrence records, and both are cited here because conclusions drawn from an overlay depend on the layer as much as on the points. Administrative boundaries — the national outline and the 38 municipalities alike — are OpenStreetMap, for the reasons set out under A note on the spatial filter below. Protected areas are the European Environment Agency’s inventory of Nationally designated areas, version 24 (July 2026).

Administrative boundaries: OpenStreetMap — national outline and 38 municipalities Licence: Open Database License (ODbL) 1.0, © OpenStreetMap contributorsSource: openstreetmap.org/copyright Protected areas: EEA Nationally designated areas (NatDA/CDDA), v24 (July 2026) DOI: https://doi.org/10.2909/028003e7-7585-4d69-92fc-7f81e0cc2340 Licence: CC-BY 4.0, © European Environment Agency Coverage for Kosovo: 237 designated sites, 48 with a mapped boundary

The land-cover screen further down adds two more layers, CORINE Land Cover and the EEA’s biogeographical regions, and cites them where they are used.






NoteA note on the spatial filter





Records were selected using the GADM administrative boundary for Kosovo (GID XKO) rather than the ISO country code XK. The GADM boundary is a true spatial filter, so it also captures records whose publisher left the country field blank or assigned it to a neighbouring state — a common situation for cross-border survey data. Queried against the GBIF occurrence API without any further filters at the time of extraction, gadmGid=XKO returned 52,290 records against 48,947 for country=XK, about 7 per cent more.
Note that the GADM identifier for Kosovo is XKO. The similar-looking code XKX is the World Bank / ISO alpha-3 style code and is not recognised by GADM — pred("gadm", "XKX") returns zero records rather than an error, so a pipeline using it would silently produce an empty dataset.
Selecting the records is not the same as defining the country. GADM’s Kosovo polygon is a generalisation: 1,210 vertices for a border that runs 743 km, roughly one point every 600 m of a line that turns far more often than that. Sampling both candidate borders every 200 m and measuring to Eurostat’s GISCO 1:1M line — an independent official digitisation of the same international border — GADM’s sits a median 587 m from it, and 2,980 m at the ninetieth percentile. OpenStreetMap’s sits 60 m and 189 m; the residual there is GISCO’s own generalisation rather than OSM’s. The areas tell the same story: published figures for Kosovo cluster between 10,887 km² (World Bank) and 10,910 km², and OpenStreetMap’s polygon measures 10,898 km², inside that range, where GADM’s measures 10,828 km², below all of it. The two outlines disagree over 755 km², 6.9 per cent of the country, and run up to 4.1 km apart.
This report therefore selects on GADM, because that is the filter GBIF offers, and screens and draws on OpenStreetMap, because that is where the border actually is. Both errors in GADM’s outline matter, and only one of them can be repaired here:

Where GADM bulges outward, it swept in 1,776 records that are not in Kosovo. Their own publishers say as much: 1,030 are stamped ME, 320 MK, 284 RS and 45 AL, against 97 stamped XK. The country-coordinate test removes them — see below.
Where GADM falls short, 412 km² of Kosovo lies outside the polygon GBIF filtered on, and records there were never in the download to begin with. Nothing downstream can recover them. Closing that gap means selecting on a geometry predicate instead, which mints a new download and a new DOI.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
text:
Summary statistics
Each row below is a distinct thematic extract of the cleaned dataset. All seven are available for download at the end of this report.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
text:
Data quality control
Aggregated occurrence data carries well-known geographic artefacts: records placed at the centre of a country, at a museum’s own address, or at coordinates of exactly zero. Every record was screened with CoordinateCleaner and only records passing all tests were retained.
The screening finds nothing to remove, and that is the expected result rather than a broken test. GBIF’s own filters excluded records without coordinates and records it had already flagged with a geospatial issue before the extract was built, and the extract was selected by a true spatial filter, so the failure modes these tests look for have no way into the dataset. The screening is kept because it is the guarantee: it would catch them if they ever appeared.












NoteWhich tests were applied, which were left out, and the polygon they all depend on





Applied: zero coordinates, country-coordinate mismatch, GBIF headquarters, known biodiversity institutions, and identical latitude/longitude values.
Deliberately not applied: the capital city and country centroid tests. Both discard records falling within a fixed radius of a capital or of a country’s geometric centre. Kosovo is small enough that Pristina and the national centroid both sit well inside the territory, so these tests would remove a large number of entirely legitimate records — including most urban biodiversity data. They can be enabled in pipeline.R by setting use_capitals_test = TRUE.
The country-coordinate test needed two corrections, and both fail silently.
It cannot see Kosovo by default. Natural Earth, the reference dataset CoordinateCleaner ships with, records Kosovo with no assigned ISO alpha-3 code. Run against that default the test flags 100 per cent of Kosovo records as mismatches and, with value = "clean", returns an empty data frame without warning. The pipeline therefore supplies a bespoke reference polygon stamped with the code used in the occurrence data.
That polygon then has to be the right one. Built from Natural Earth’s 1:50m outline — 72 vertices for the whole country, straying up to 4.7 km from the true border — the test flagged 1,296 records on the strength of the outline’s own error. Built from GADM level 0, the polygon GBIF filters on, it flagged nothing at all, which looks like a clean bill of health and is in fact the test grading its own paper: every record lies inside that polygon by construction, so asking whether it does can only ever return yes.
The reference is now the OpenStreetMap outline, which is neither the coarse polygon nor the selecting one, and the test does what it is for. It flags 1,776 records, 3.7 per cent of those with coordinates. These are not borderline calls made by a wobbly line: 94 per cent of them carry a publisher-assigned country code of ME, MK, RS or AL, and they sit a median 552 m and up to 3.3 km beyond the border. They are the records GADM’s outward bulges swept into the download, and removing them is the point of the exercise.
The correction is not free. 235 species leave the dataset with them, having been recorded nowhere else in the extract. Most probably do occur in Kosovo — they were found a few hundred metres the wrong side of a line — but this extract no longer claims evidence that they do, which is the honest position for it to take.
Records within a set distance of the border can be kept instead by setting country_buffer in pipeline.R; it is NULL here, meaning a strict test.




How precisely are the records placed?
Passing the coordinate tests means a record is not obviously wrong. It does not mean the record is precise enough for every purpose. A great many Kosovo records come from atlas-style surveys that report to a 10 km square, and the stated coordinate uncertainty is the honest way to tell those apart from a GPS-located field observation.












NoteWhy coarse records are kept rather than filtered out





The GBIF Viewer developed for Ukraine discards records whose stated uncertainty exceeds a threshold, on the reasonable grounds that a record placed to the nearest 10 km cannot support a decision about a particular field.
Applied here with a 1 km threshold, that rule would remove 20 per cent of the records. If records that state no uncertainty at all were dropped as well, since they cannot show that they are precise, it would remove 89 per cent. 18 per cent carry an uncertainty of exactly 7,071 m, which is the half-diagonal of a 10 km square: these are atlas records, and they are perfectly good evidence that a species occurs in a landscape even though they say nothing about where in it. Discarding them would make the country look emptier than it is, which is the more dangerous error for conservation planning.
The pipeline therefore reports the precision profile, keeps coordinateUncertaintyInMeters in every export, and offers precision as a filter in the record explorer below. The threshold is available as coord_uncertainty_max in pipeline.R for anyone who does want it applied. Which precision is enough depends on the decision; the Natura 2000 questions page sets out three tiers, from national screening to the Standard Data Form.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
text:
Where the records are
Each map carries the same set of switchable layers, reached through the control in the top-right corner:

Occurrence records — individual records, clustered until you zoom in, each with a pop-up carrying the determination, the place, the stated accuracy and a link through to the record on GBIF, where the evidence and any photographs can be checked. Where a tab holds more than 10,000 records this layer is left off altogether rather than thinned to a sample, because a thinned layer of dots looks exactly like a thin one; the two density layers below then carry the same records, and the explorer further down maps them one at a time.
Record density — every record aggregated onto a 2 km grid and classed against a legend. This is the layer to read when the question is how many.
Heat map — the same information as a smooth surface, better for seeing the shape of the sampled and unsampled areas.
Protected areas — the nationally designated sites, shown as a green wash under the records so that whether a record falls inside one can be read at a glance. Hovering names the site, its designation, its size and how much has been recorded there. Two further layers sit alongside it in the control: the strict protection zones inside the larger sites, and the 189 natural monuments — veteran trees, springs and caves — that the register records as a point rather than a boundary.
Municipalities — administrative boundaries, with each unit’s own record and species count on hover.

The toolbar on the left adds full-screen, a distance and area measure, a polygon and rectangle sketching tool, and a place search, so an area of interest can be outlined and sized directly on the map.

All biodiversityBirdsBirds Directive, Annex IHabitats DirectiveHabitats Directive, Annex IIIUCN threatenedInvasive alien species



























































Both density layers are the more informative reading of survey effort. Dense cells frequently mark well-visited sites rather than exceptionally rich ones, and pale areas usually indicate that nobody has yet surveyed there. Both readings matter when prioritising future fieldwork.






NoteHow the density layers are built, and why the heat map changed





Occurrence counts are extraordinarily uneven. Rounded to about 110 m, Kosovo has 5,590 occupied positions; three quarters of them hold a single record, and the busiest holds more than thirteen thousand. Any display that treats that range naively collapses.
The heat map previously did exactly that. Leaflet’s heat layer draws each point at an opacity of intensity / max and then colours the accumulated opacity through a gradient, so feeding it raw counts made every occupied cell saturate identically. Two further defaults compounded it: a minimum-opacity floor that lifted empty-ish areas up to the same value as real clusters, and an internal zoom scaling that divides every intensity by 2^(maxZoom - currentZoom) — about a thousandfold at the country view — pushing the whole surface onto that floor. The result was a single flat wash.
The layer now: aggregates onto the 110 m grid; maps the counts onto 0–1 with a logarithmic transform followed by a power below one, which spreads the crowded bottom of the distribution across usable values; pins the zoom reference so the surface means the same thing at every scale; and uses GBIF’s own density ramp, the one the occurrence map on gbif.org draws with. It runs yellow to red rather than through a single hue, but it darkens at every step, so “more” still reads as “darker” rather than as “a different colour” — which is the property a rainbow lacks and the reason one is not used here.
The Record density grid is the same information without the smoothing: 2 km cells, classed on roughly logarithmic breaks, with a legend and the exact count on hover. Use the heat map to see the shape of the coverage and the grid when a number is needed.









NoteAbout the common names shown in the pop-ups





Common names are not part of the GBIF download and are retrieved separately from the GBIF species API, which returns every name any publisher has supplied. The pipeline takes the most frequently published English name for each taxon, which recovers the standard name in the large majority of cases.
Publishers do, however, mis-tag the language of their names fairly often — roughly a fifth of the names returned as English for this dataset were in fact Norwegian, German, French, Swedish, Hungarian or Ukrainian. Names written in non-Latin scripts are filtered out automatically, but a mis-tagged Latin-script name occasionally survives. The scientific name is always the authoritative identifier; treat the common name as a convenience only.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
text:
Survey coverage by municipality
The map above answers “where are the records”. This one answers the question a planning authority actually asks: how well is my municipality covered? Records are counted per unit of area, because a large municipality with a moderate number of records may be far less well known than a small one with fewer.


















WarningOne municipality dominates the totals — read it carefully





Graçanicë / Gračanica holds far more records per square kilometre than anywhere else in the country. That is not a statement about its biodiversity. A single coordinate inside it carries more than thirteen thousand records, almost all of them bird observations submitted to one citizen-science platform from what is in practice one regularly watched site.
This is the characteristic shape of aggregated occurrence data and the reason raw record counts should never be read as species richness. The species column in the table above is the more honest comparison, and the two rank very differently: Graçanicë leads on records and sits well down the table on species.
That coordinate also shows why the municipal layer had to be replaced along with the national outline. It sits in the countryside south of Prishtina, on ground that belonged to Fushë Kosovë until the 2010 decentralisation moved it into the newly created municipality of Graçanicë. GADM 4.1 still draws the pre-2010 map, so every one of those thirteen thousand records used to be attributed to Fushë Kosovë — the wrong municipality, and the one a reader would have gone looking in.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
text:
Protected areas
A record’s value to conservation depends partly on where it falls. A population inside a national park is already covered by a management regime and a competent authority; the same population on undesignated ground is not. This section lays the occurrence data over Kosovo’s protected-area network and reports what each contains.
The network is taken from the European Environment Agency’s inventory of Nationally designated areas (NatDA, long known as the Common Database on Designated Areas, CDDA). This is the channel through which 38 Eionet countries report their protected areas to the World Database on Protected Areas, so Kosovo’s entry is its own official register rather than a third-party compilation.


237Designated sites


1,261 km²Protected network


11.6%Of the national territory


21,069Records inside a site


45%Of all records


2,262Species inside a site


21,069 of the 46,831 quality-checked records — 45 per cent — fall inside a designated site, and they carry 2,262 species between them. Against a network covering 11.6 per cent of the country that looks like a striking concentration, and it is worth taking apart before it is believed.
Most of it is one place. Ligatina e Hencit/ Radevës, a wetland of 1.10 km², supplies 13,346 of those records on its own — 63 per cent of everything inside the network, from 0.09 per cent of its area. Set that single site aside and 7,723 of the remaining 33,485 records fall in a protected area, 23 per cent against an 11.6 per cent share of the land.
Roughly twice the records per unit area, then, rather than five times — a real concentration, but a modest one, and it says as much about where people go to look as about what lives there. The section on survey coverage makes the same point in administrative units.

What the register contains






Kosovo’s register holds 237 designated sites, and it comes in two shapes. 48 carry a mapped boundary; the other 189 are recorded as a single point. That split is not a gap in the data — it is what the sites are. Every national park, strict nature reserve, protected landscape, nature park and wetland is a polygon. The point-only sites are all natural monuments, which in Kosovo means individual veteran trees, springs and caves, most of them smaller than a tenth of a hectare. A point is an honest way to record a stand of oak; a polygon would imply a precision the register does not claim.
A further 19 features are strict-protection zones — the strictly protected cores of sites the table already lists, not separate sites. They hold 762 records. Their area and their records are contained in the rows above rather than additional to them, which is why they are labelled as a role rather than counted as sites, and why the columns in that table must not be added up.


Which sites hold the evidence






Counted by site, the coverage looks thin: 28 of the 48 sites with a mapped boundary hold no quality-checked GBIF record at all. Counted by area, it looks the opposite — those 28 sites come to 4.17 km² between them, 0.3 per cent of the mapped network, and the remaining 99.7 per cent does have records.
Both readings are true, and the difference between them is the finding. The gaps are almost entirely in the small sites: 26 of the 28 are natural monuments, and the median one covers 0.017 km². Every national park, the nature park and the wetland are recorded in; it is the municipal-scale sites that are not.
The strict-protection zones are the sharper gap. These are the most tightly protected ground in the country, and 7 of the 19 hold no record — 12.3 km² of the 108.9 km² under strict protection, 11 per cent of it, with no openly published occurrence evidence behind it.
A site with no records is not a site with no species; it is a site nobody has surveyed, or one whose surveys were never published to GBIF. Which of the two it is, is worth knowing before the next field season is planned — and for the small municipal sites in particular, a single visit would produce the first open record either way.






WarningThree ways to misread this table





The IUCN column is not the Red List. It is the IUCN protected-area management category — Ia, Ib, II, III, V — which says how a site is run, not how likely anything in it is to go extinct. The Red List categories used elsewhere in this report are CR, EN, VU and so on. The two share an acronym and nothing else.
Records per square kilometre measure effort, not richness. The wetland at the top of that column carries more than twelve thousand records in barely a square kilometre, almost all of them bird observations submitted to one citizen-science platform from what is in practice one regularly watched spot. It is the same concentration described under survey coverage, seen through a different boundary. The species column is the more honest comparison.
The point-only sites hold no records here, and cannot. A point has no inside, so the 189 natural monuments recorded that way can never match a record by point-in-polygon, however well surveyed they are. They appear on the maps above, and in the published register, but they are absent from this table by construction rather than for want of evidence.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
section: Potential Natura 2000 habitats: a land-cover screen
text:
Potential Natura 2000 habitats: a land-cover screen
The sections above ask where species have been recorded. A Natura 2000 network is judged as much on its habitats: whether it holds enough of each natural habitat type listed in Annex I of the Habitats Directive. A gap analysis starts with two questions. Where could those habitats occur? And how much of that ground already lies inside a designated site? Kosovo has no habitat map to answer them with yet (question 3 on the Natura 2000 page sets out what one would take), so this section answers them from land cover instead.


7,534 km²Potential habitat


69%Of the national territory


16.6%Inside a designated site


6,281 km²Outside every site


48 / 237Sites with an area to count


CORINE Land Cover 2018 maps 7,534 km² of Kosovo, or 69 per cent of the country, as natural or semi-natural cover that could hold an Annex I habitat. Of that, 16.6 per cent lies inside a designated site. The other 6,281 km² does not, and that is the gap the map below draws hatched.
The gap is not spread evenly, and the reason is where the network lies. The Alpine biogeographical region covers the mountain rim along the western and southern borders: Bjeshkët e Nemuna, the Šar Mountains and Pashtrik. It is 19 per cent of Kosovo, and 58 per cent of its potential habitat is already designated. The Continental region is the other 81 per cent, and there the figure is 4 per cent. Kosovo’s network is, in effect, a mountain network. The lowland and hill forests, the grasslands and the scrub make up most of the potential habitat by area, and almost all of them lie outside it.
The same pattern shows in the crosswalk’s confidence levels, because the confident classes are the mountain ones: alpine grassland, heath and bare rock. Of the high-confidence potential habitat, 51 per cent is designated, against 15 per cent of the medium-confidence classes (almost all forest) and 9 per cent of the low-confidence ones.

Why land cover is only a proxy
CORINE Land Cover (CLC) is a European inventory of land cover, interpreted from satellite imagery by national teams to a common 44-class nomenclature. It is the best consistent layer available for the whole country, and it is the wrong kind of layer for this question in five ways:

Small habitats disappear. CLC maps nothing smaller than 25 hectares or narrower than 100 metres. Springs, fens, small mires, riparian strips and rock outcrops are absorbed into whatever surrounds them, and several of the Annex I types most in need of site protection are exactly these. The 1.3 km² of wetland on this map is what a 25 ha unit can see. It is a floor, not an estimate.
Land cover is not vegetation type. “Broad-leaved forest” is one class whether it is a montane beech wood, a thermophilous oak coppice or an alluvial alder stand. Those are different Annex I types, or no Annex I type at all. The crosswalk therefore offers several candidates for each class and never picks one.
Forest classes include plantations. A conifer plantation and a natural spruce forest are the same class, 312.
Pastures cannot be told apart by how they are managed. Class 231 holds fertilised, reseeded grassland as well as the species-rich hay meadows of types 6510 and 6520, and only the second kind qualifies. Class 243, a mosaic of fields with fragments of natural vegetation, is the same problem at a finer grain.
Some water bodies are reservoirs. CLC files a reservoir under the same class as a natural lake. Eight of Kosovo’s eleven mapped water bodies are reservoirs, among them Gazivoda/Ujmani, Radoniq, Batllava and Badovc, and they are left out. The other three could not be identified either way and stay in at low confidence.

The areas themselves are sound. Every figure in this section is measured on the full CLC geometry in EPSG:3035, the equal-area projection CLC is produced in. The totals by habitat group, by confidence and by municipality all reconcile to within a hundredth of a per cent. What needs the field is the interpretation, not the arithmetic.


The map
The map has the same toolbar and the same layer control as the maps above, and five overlays of its own, listed here in the order they are drawn:

CORINE Land Cover 2018 (all classes): every class, in the official CLC colours, as the EEA’s own map service draws it. Off by default. Unlike the other layers it is not cut at the border.
Potential natural habitats: the land cover the crosswalk keeps, coloured by habitat group. Confidence shows as strength of fill: a solid colour is a class the crosswalk is sure of, and a faint one a class it doubts. Hover over a polygon for its class, its size and which site it is in. Click it for the candidate Annex I types.
Protected areas: the designated sites, drawn here as outlines so the habitat colours beneath them stay true.
Gap: potential habitat outside designated sites: hatched. This is the layer the section is about.
Municipalities: each with its own gap on hover. Switch it off again to get back to the habitat polygons underneath.









How much of each habitat group is designated






The biogeographical seminars that review Natura 2000 proposals have long used rough reference values. A network holding 60 per cent or more of a habitat type’s national area is taken as likely sufficient, and one holding less than 20 per cent as likely insufficient. The table sets each group against those values as an orientation only, for two reasons. First, the thresholds apply to Annex I habitat types, one at a time, against a mapped national total. A habitat group here is several land-cover classes, each standing for several Annex I types or none, so a group’s share cannot show that any one habitat type is well or badly covered. Second, the seminars themselves never used the values on their own. What the table can show is where the network’s hold on natural land is thin enough that a type-by-type analysis will probably find gaps. On forest and grassland, the two groups that make up most of the potential habitat, it is. Question 4 on the Natura 2000 page sets out how to do the type-by-type analysis before a national habitat map exists.


Where the gap is, by municipality












NoteThe crosswalk from land cover to Annex I, and how to correct it





Everything on this map that is a judgement rather than a measurement sits in one file, data/crosswalk_clc_annex1.csv, with one row per CLC class. It is a draft for specialist review. The table below shows the rows that keep land cover, with the Directive’s own name for each candidate type, read from the legal text so that a mistyped code is caught rather than published. An asterisk marks a priority habitat type.






Confidence is the crosswalk’s view of how often a class holds any of its candidate types:

high: most of the class is one of the candidates. Examples are natural grassland and bare rock in the mountains.
medium: the candidates are likely, but mixed with cover that qualifies as none of them, as with managed and plantation forest.
low: the class holds a qualifying habitat only in part, or only under a particular kind of management that CLC cannot see. Pastures, farm mosaics, transitional scrub and open water are here.

Confidence is shown on the map as strength of colour rather than used as a filter. potential_habitat_min_confidence in pipeline.R is set to “low”, which keeps every class, so a reader sees the doubtful ground rather than being spared it.
The status column was added for this report. The draft crosswalk named classes, groups, candidates and confidence levels. Whether a class is natural (not maintained by use) or semi-natural (shaped by forestry, grazing or abandonment) was assigned here, so it is a reviewable choice like the rest.
Four doubts are recorded in the notes rather than acted on. Annex I holds types specific to the central Balkans that the draft does not list: Moesian beech forests (91W0), Moesian silver fir forests (91BA), Oro-Moesian acidophilous grasslands (62D0), and species-rich Nardus grasslands (6230*). Whether any of them belongs in a row is for a specialist to decide, so the notes flag them and no code has been added.
One of natural land cover in Kosovo class is not handled by the draft: Burnt areas (334), 16.4 km² in 15 polygons. It is left out of the potential habitat, and the note on the row asks for a decision. Burnt ground may well be forest or grassland that will grow back.
Sclerophyllous vegetation (323) turns up, but it is not real. The draft asks for any occurrence to be reported. There are eight polygons with 1.1 hectares between them, all along the southern border. They are the edges of polygons mapped on the Albanian and North Macedonian side, clipped a few metres inside the OpenStreetMap outline where the two borders disagree. The widest of them is 22 m across.
Eight polygons are reclassified by name. They are the reservoirs CLC files as water bodies. Each is listed in data/clc_polygon_overrides.csv with the OpenStreetMap feature or dam that identifies it:






How to correct it. Edit a row of the CSV, or open an issue saying which row is wrong and why. The next run of pipeline.R redraws the map and recomputes every figure in this section. Where a class stands for different habitat types in the two regions, add a second row for the class with biogeo_region set to Alpine or Continental. That row then applies in that region and the general row everywhere else, so a different list of candidates for alpine grassland needs no code.





What this is evidence for, and what comes next
This is national-screening evidence, the first of the three tiers set out under question 1 on the Natura 2000 page. It is good enough to decide where to look, and not good enough to draw a boundary or to fill in a Standard Data Form. Nothing on this map is an Annex I habitat until somebody has stood in it. Three steps would move it on:

Verify the high-confidence gap in the field. Of the high-confidence potential habitat, 373 km² lies outside every site. Those classes are the ones most likely to be what they seem, so a sample of those polygons, visited and recorded to the mapping standard under question 3, would test the crosswalk where it claims most.
Split the classes by elevation. A terrain model such as the Copernicus DEM would separate montane beech from thermophilous oak, and alpine grassland from lowland pasture. Most classes could then carry one or two candidate types instead of up to seven, and the crosswalk would gain the elevation bands it now leaves in its notes.
Lay the directive-listed records over the gap. The Annex II species and Annex I birds recorded in this report can be intersected with the gap polygons to rank them. A gap polygon holding a listed species is a stronger candidate for designation than one that holds none.


Land cover: CORINE Land Cover 2018 (vector), Europe, 6-yearly, version V2020_20u1 (May 2020) DOI: https://doi.org/10.2909/71c95a07-e296-44fc-b22b-415f42acfdf0 Licence: Copernicus data and information policy: full, free and open access under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No 1159/2013 Attribution: Generated using European Union’s Copernicus Land Monitoring Service information; https://doi.org/10.2909/71c95a07-e296-44fc-b22b-415f42acfdf0 Accessed: 29 September 2026, through the EEA map service. Clipped to the national outline, reclassified through the crosswalk and simplified for display. The screen is not endorsed by the European Union or the EEA.
