title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
section: Species protected under the EU Nature Directives
text:
Species protected under the EU Nature Directives
The annex lists were taken directly from the consolidated legal texts on EUR-Lex — 193 taxa on Birds Directive Annex I, and 1,333 across Habitats Directive Annexes II, IV and V — and every name was resolved against the GBIF backbone taxonomy so that records published under superseded names are still found. Larus minutus, for instance, is listed under that name but recorded as Hydrocoloeus minutus.
The table below shows the species of Community interest that have been recorded in Kosovo. The annexes are EU-wide lists dominated by Iberian, Alpine and Macaronesian endemics, so a listed species with no records here usually lies outside its natural range rather than indicating a survey gap; the meaningful gaps are the Balkan species one would expect to find and doesn’t.












WarningHow annex membership was determined





The species lists are built by R/build_directive_list.R, which parses the consolidated directives on EUR-Lex — the legally binding texts — rather than relying on a secondary checklist. Every name is then resolved against the GBIF backbone taxonomy, and occurrence records are selected by numeric key rather than by name, which is robust to synonymy and authorship variation.
Three details materially affect what appears in these subsets.
Rank matters when matching. A taxon listed at species rank is matched on both its species key and its taxon key, so records identified to subspecies are still captured. A taxon listed at subspecies rank is matched on that subspecies alone. Promoting subspecies listings to their whole species would be seriously misleading: the Birds Directive lists island endemics such as Columba palumbus azorica and Fringilla coelebs ombriosa, and matching those at species level would place every Wood Pigeon and Chaffinch in Kosovo on Annex I — around 1,450 records for subspecies confined to the Azores and the Canaries.
Lumped species are not followed. Some listed species have since been sunk into a widespread one. The GBIF backbone files Dactylorhiza kalopissii under D. majalis, Capra aegagrus under the domestic goat, Polyommatus eroides under P. eros and Apatura metis under A. ilia. Following those synonyms would put every record of the widespread species on the annex, so these listings are matched only on records that carry the listed name itself. A synonym that just moves a species to another genus, such as Egretta alba to Ardea alba, is still followed.
Exclusions are honoured. Where an annex lists a species except certain subspecies, as Annex V does for Rupicapra rupicapra, the excluded taxa are discarded rather than being read as listings in their own right.
Around 1.3 per cent of annex entries could not be resolved to a current GBIF taxon. These are names superseded since the directives were adopted, mostly Iberian and Macaronesian plants; none are species expected in Kosovo. The directive and annex columns are retained in every export so that any selection can be checked.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
section: Extinction risk: the IUCN Red List
text:
Extinction risk: the IUCN Red List
The EU annexes say what is legally protected. The IUCN Red List says what is at risk of extinction. The two overlap only partly, and a screening exercise needs both: a species can be at serious risk without appearing on any annex, and much of what is annexed is of least concern globally.
Every species in the dataset was matched to its global Red List assessment through the GBIF backbone taxonomy.


















NoteReading these assessments with care





Two cautions apply.
The assessment is global, not national. A species of least concern across Europe may be on the edge of its range and genuinely rare in Kosovo, and nothing in this table would show it. A national red list is the instrument for that question; this is a screen, not a substitute.
Backbone matching can misfire. The Red List category is attached through the GBIF backbone taxonomy, which occasionally links a name to an assessment of a different taxon. One record in this dataset is attributed to a species assessed as Extinct, which for a beetle collected in the Balkans is far more likely to be a taxonomic mismatch than a rediscovery. Treat a surprising category as a question to check rather than as a finding.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
section: Invasive alien species of Union concern
text:
Invasive alien species of Union concern
The directives and the Red List say what is at stake. Regulation (EU) No 1143/2014 deals with one of the things that puts it at risk: invasive alien species, introduced by people outside their natural range, that damage the ecosystems they spread into. Its core is the Union list — species that may not be imported, kept, bred, sold or released anywhere in the EU, for which Member States must run surveillance, report every new finding and act on it early, and manage populations that are already widespread.
The Regulation binds EU Member States. As with the Nature Directives elsewhere in this report, it is used here as the reference list against which the evidence is screened, not as a statement of what applies in Kosovo today.


114Species on the Union list


5Recorded in Kosovo


24Records


2Inside a designated site


20Across the border, not recorded here


Of the 114 species on the list, five have any quality-checked record in Kosovo, and they have 24 records between them. Twelve of the records date from 2015 or later, every one of them through iNaturalist.org and Pl@ntNet — citizen science, in other words, rather than survey. The other twelve either predate 2000 or carry no date; they come from Freshwater fishes of the Western Balkans, Small mammals of Yugoslavia 1992 atlas and Freshwater fishes of Serbia and Montenegro.
Read that as a statement about recording, not about the country. Tree of heaven, the most-recorded of the five, has eight records here and 406 across the four neighbouring countries, 242 of them in Serbia. Invasive species are what recorders walk past: the widespread ones are too familiar to note, and few surveys set out to find them. An absence from the table below is therefore no evidence that a species is absent from Kosovo — and for this list that is the expensive mistake to make, because a species caught early is the only kind that can still be eradicated.






Two of the records fall inside a designated site: muskrat in Ligatina e Hencit/ Radevës (2025) and stone moroko in Mali Pashtrik dhe Liqeni i Vërmices (1992). A record inside a protected area is the one a site manager needs to hear about first. Every record is in the explorer below, under the EU invasive species filter.

The watch list: across the border, not yet recorded here
The Regulation is built around early detection, and the species most likely to be found in Kosovo next are the ones already established next door. The table below lists every Union-list species with records in at least one neighbouring country and none in this extract, most widespread first.












NoteHow the Union list was built, and how the watch list was counted





The list is taken from the legal texts. R/build_ias_list.R reads the consolidated Implementing Regulation (EU) 2016/1141 and the four acts that amended it, and resolves every name against the GBIF backbone. The list holds 114 species. 111 apply today; the other 3 were listed with a deferred date — Castor canadensis from 7 August 2027, Celastrus orbiculatus from 2 August 2027, Neogale vison from 7 August 2027 — and are kept here, since a screen should catch them before the date rather than after it. The consolidated text on its own would have missed all three: a consolidated version carries only what already applies.
It agrees with the checklist published on GBIF, species for species. The Research Institute for Nature and Forest (INBO) publishes the Union list as a checklist dataset (doi:10.15468/97aucj), and unlike the per-annex Nature Directive checklists on GBIF, which leave out species beyond the region they were compiled for, it is complete. It supplies the English names in the tables. It is not the source, because its names are linked to the GBIF backbone less well than they are chosen: two of its species have no backbone link at all, one because a single accent (“Triadica sebífera”) defeats GBIF’s name parser, and one for the reason in the next paragraph.
One listed name does not exist in the GBIF backbone. The 2025 amendment lists the American mink as Neogale vison, the genus it was moved to in 2021. Asked for that name, GBIF’s matching service returns the genus Neogale, which it holds as a synonym of Mustela — a “higher rank” match, at 94 per cent confidence, and no error. Taken at face value, that would put every native weasel, stoat and polecat on the list of invasive species. The build refuses such matches rather than quietly promoting a species listing to a whole genus, and resolves the mink through its former name to Mustela vison, where the backbone holds it.
Three listings are below species rank — Vespa velutina nigrithorax, Procambarus fallax f. virginalis and Pueraria montana var. lobata — and each is matched on its whole species. That is the opposite of the rule for the Birds Directive’s island subspecies, and deliberately so: each of these is the form of its species that is established in Europe, and most records are identified to species only.
The watch list is a dated screening aid, not evidence of the same standard as the rest of this report. The counts come from the GBIF occurrence API with the download’s own quality filters, counted on 28 September 2026, and they are not covered by the DOI above. The neighbours are selected by their GADM boundaries, which draw Serbia without Kosovo, so no record inside Kosovo is counted as Serbian. A record across the border may be a planted tree, a pond turtle or a museum specimen; check the records on GBIF before treating any one of them as an established population.

TipConditions of use



GBIF-mediated data are made available under the licences chosen by each publishing institution; the license column in every export records the terms applying to each record. When these data are used in a report or publication, please cite the DOI given above, which credits all contributing institutions.
The protected-area boundaries are © European Environment Agency and are redistributed here under CC-BY 4.0, which requires attribution and permits reuse for any purpose. Cite them as https://doi.org/10.2909/028003e7-7585-4d69-92fc-7f81e0cc2340.

Any reuse should carry the line “Generated using European Union’s Copernicus Land Monitoring Service information; https://doi.org/10.2909/71c95a07-e296-44fc-b22b-415f42acfdf0”, state that it was clipped to Kosovo and reclassified through the crosswalk, and cite the biogeographical regions, © EEA, under CC-BY 4.0.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
text:
Methods and reproducibility
The entire analysis is scripted and version-controlled. To reproduce it:

Install the R packages listed below.
Add your GBIF credentials to .Renviron (see the repository README.md).
Run Rscript pipeline.R to acquire, clean, enrich and export the data.
Run quarto render to rebuild this website.

pipeline.R records its GBIF download key, so re-running it re-uses the existing DOI rather than minting a new one. Delete data/gbif_download/download_key.txt to force a fresh extract. The vernacular name, Red List and dataset-registry lookups are cached under data/, so only the first run makes those requests; so are the neighbouring-country counts behind the invasive-species watch list, which is why that table states the day they were taken.
The two species lists are built from the legal texts, by Rscript R/build_directive_list.R for the Nature Directive annexes and Rscript R/build_ias_list.R for the Union list of invasive alien species. Both write a CSV that is kept in the repository, so neither needs running again until the legislation changes.
The land-cover screen needs no account. By default pipeline.R reads CORINE Land Cover 2018 for Kosovo from the EEA’s map service, clips it to the national outline, and caches the extract as data/kosovo_clc2018.gpkg. Delete that file to read it again. To use a file from the Copernicus portal instead:

Sign in at land.copernicus.eu with an EU Login and download the vector product of the vintage (GeoPackage or File Geodatabase). The raster will not do.
Unzip it anywhere outside the repository. The file is large and only the Kosovo extract is ever written back.
Point CLC_PATH in .Renviron at the .gpkg or .gdb, or set clc_path in pipeline.R, delete the cached extract, and run the pipeline. It reads only the part of the file that covers Kosovo. If the path is set and nothing is there, it stops and says what to download.

Three more parameters in pipeline.R control the screen. clc_vintage chooses the CLC edition, and is refused unless its DOI, version and licence are recorded in R/functions.R. clc_simplify_tolerance sets the display generalisation, 50 m here. potential_habitat_min_confidence sets the lowest crosswalk confidence kept, “low” here. The judgements themselves are not parameters: they are the rows of data/crosswalk_clc_annex1.csv and data/clc_polygon_overrides.csv.

title: GIS and biodiversity data management
text: This page gathers the material from the six sessions Jonáš Gaigr of the Nature Conservation Agency of the Czech Republic gave at the mission. Every presentation is here as slides to view in the browser and as a PDF handout to download, next to the GBIF data site that several of the sessions used as their worked example.

title: GIS and biodiversity data management
text:
The mission
The Expert Mission on Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and biodiversity data management was organised by TAIEX, the European Commission’s Technical Assistance and Information Exchange instrument, in co-operation with the Ministry of Environment, Spatial Planning and Infrastructure (case ID ETT IND/EXP 82606). For three days, experts from the Nature Conservation Agency of the Czech Republic and the Ministry of Environment of the Slovak Republic worked with the institutions that hold Kosovo’s* biodiversity data.
Its aim was practical: to show how GIS supports environmental management, biodiversity conservation and the implementation of the Birds and Habitats Directives. That covered spatial analysis, habitat mapping, satellite and remote sensing data, the monitoring of protected areas, assessing the conservation status of habitats and species, and identifying Natura 2000 sites. Alongside it, the mission set out to bring spatial data management in line with EU standards and to strengthen co-operation between the institutions that collect and use the data.

* This designation is without prejudice to positions on status, and is in line with UNSCR 1244/1999 and the ICJ Opinion on the Kosovo declaration of independence.

title: Towards Natura 2000
text:
The Ministry put a set of questions to the expert team about moving from Kosovo’s present biodiversity data towards a Natura 2000 network. This page answers them as far as they fall within five sessions of the mission: spatial analysis, condition evaluation, GBIF data, field data collection and automated reporting. How sites are proposed, how Article 17 reporting works and how the institutions divide the work are the subject of the sessions by Karel Chobot and Martin Koška, and are not answered here. The numbering follows the Ministry’s list; question 7 lies outside these sessions.
Each answer gives the recommendation first, then what Kosovo’s own data show about it. Those figures are computed from the same GBIF extract, protected-area register and pipeline as the main report, so they move with it.

title: Towards Natura 2000
section: 1. Which data are good enough for which decision
text:
1. Which data are good enough for which decision
Treat fitness for use as a property of each record, computed by a written rule, in three tiers: national screening, candidate-site delineation and the Standard Data Form (SDF). A record moves up a tier by gaining precision, currency, documentation and validation, never because the decision it is wanted for is more important.










National screening
Candidate-site delineation
Standard Data Form




Spatial precision
Within the screening cell; 10 km atlas records for 10 km screening only
Points to 100 m or better; habitat polygons mapped at 1:10,000
As for delineation, and tied to a survey unit: plot, transect, polygon


Currency
Any date; records before 2000 flagged as historical
Observed within the last 12 years, two six-year reporting cycles
From a standardised survey, ideally within the current reporting cycle


Documentation
A citable source (dataset DOI or reference); name resolved against a taxonomic backbone
+ observer, date and method; a photograph or specimen for difficult taxa
+ survey protocol, effort, and counts with their units


Validation
Automated: coordinates, country, outliers, name matching
Verified by a named specialist for the taxonomic group
+ checked at site level, and given an SDF data-quality code: G, M, P or VP


Can support
Where to look; gap analysis; survey planning
Drawing and justifying a boundary
The population, area and assessment fields of the SDF



The values are proposals for national agreement, not established standards. Keep them as rows in a table rather than sentences in a guideline, so that moving a threshold is a one-line change anyone can review, and the tier of every record can be recomputed when it moves.
Two rules hold at every tier. A missing record is not evidence of absence; only surveys that record effort and non-detections can support one. And a name resolved by a backbone can still be the wrong taxon: synonymy in a global backbone can fold a Balkan endemic into a widespread species, or a domestic animal into its wild ancestor. A record whose name changed during matching is one for a specialist to look at.

What Kosovo’s data show












Records
All

… and observed since 2014
… and observer named

By these rules, 5.6 % of GBIF records could support a boundary, and even those still need a specialist’s verification. No GBIF record reaches the SDF tier on its own: the extract carries neither a survey protocol nor a measure of effort, and that tier needs both.
The Annex I bird row shows why the tiers matter. 82 % of Kosovo’s Annex I bird records come from eBird, which publishes the checklist’s location without a stated uncertainty. For a stationary count at a wetland that point is close to the birds; for a travelling checklist they may be kilometres away. The rule cannot tell the two apart, so it places both at the screening tier until the effort fields are read from eBird’s own dataset (question 6).
For Natura 2000 purposes GBIF is a screening layer, and a good one: it says where the evidence is and where it is missing. The precision profile in the main report gives the full distribution.
Discussed in: GBIF data (Day 2), “How precisely are the records placed?”; Field data collection (Day 3), “What a form enforces at the point of capture”. A 15 m accuracy constraint on the device makes a new record delineation-grade at the moment it is captured.

title: Towards Natura 2000
section: 2. From the screening grid to a site boundary
text:
2. From the screening grid to a site boundary
The grid says where to look; the boundary comes from the ground. Use the 5 × 5 km cells to rank where evidence concentrates, then discard the cell edges entirely. Draw the candidate boundary from ecological and physical units at 1:10,000, and record the reason for each stretch of it.

Screen. Score the cells from screening-tier evidence: listed features, records, survey effort. Keep the evidence score and the effort count in separate columns, so that a cell that is merely well visited is not mistaken for one that is rich.
Form search areas. Merge adjacent priority cells and buffer them generously. This is an analysis envelope, never a draft boundary; from here on, cell edges play no part.
Assemble the ecological layers inside it. Annex I habitat polygons from field mapping (question 3); the habitat around delineation-grade species records, which means breeding and feeding areas and not just the point; catchments and a terrain model; Copernicus land-cover layers; roads and settlements as barriers.
Draw along those units. Use a habitat edge, a watershed, a forest-stand edge or a river. Snap the line to features visible on the orthophoto or the cadastre at 1:10,000, so that it can be found on the ground and in the land register.
Record why. Give every boundary segment a boundary_basis attribute: habitat edge, watershed, road, cadastral parcel, expert judgement. A boundary whose reasons are written down can be defended; one whose reasons are not will be reopened at every consultation.
Test it automatically. Flag any candidate whose boundary runs along grid lines for more than a small share of its length (10 % is a reasonable start). Flag any long straight segment that follows no mapped feature. A site shaped like its screening cells fails the test by construction.
Check what the line leaves out. Run the site evidence report on the candidate polygon and a 1 km ring around it. Records just outside a boundary are the best guide to what it has cut off.

Keep the grid for what it does well: screening, planning surveys and, later, the distribution maps of Article 17-style reporting. Store every record at its own precision and derive the grid from it, never the reverse. The one exception is an atlas record, whose true precision is the cell.

What Kosovo’s data show
Ligatina e Hencit/Radevës is the country’s richest site for Annex I birds, and its designated polygon covers 1.1 km². Inside it, GBIF holds 2,408 Annex I bird records of 43 species. Within 5 km outside it lie a further 633 records of 34 species, about 21 % of all the Annex I bird records in and around the site. 5 of those species were never recorded inside. The richest locality in that ring, “M9 Bridge over Sitnica River”, lies 2.2 km from the boundary and holds 25 Annex I species.
The birds use more of the landscape than the designated wetland. An SPA boundary copied from the national designation, or from a screening cell, would leave that out. The ring in step 7 is what shows it.
Discussed in: Spatial analysis (Day 1), “Fragmentation: connection, not just cover”; Automated reporting (Day 3), “A pilot, end to end”. Karel Chobot’s case study (Day 1) covers how the Czech sites were proposed.

title: Towards Natura 2000
section: 3. Mapping Annex I habitats before assessing them
text:
3. Mapping Annex I habitats before assessing them
Several Annex III criteria need both an area and a condition, and only a polygon map carries both. These include representativity, relative surface, and the degree of conservation of structure and function. Points, localities and centroids say where to map first; they cannot be summed into an area. Map in the field at 1:10,000, record condition as attributes scored by a written rule, and validate a random sample independently before any figure goes into an assessment.








Element
Recommended minimum
Czech practice, for comparison




Base and scale
Field mapping on a colour orthophoto, drawn at 1:10,000 (1:5,000 where detail requires)
Orthophoto at 1:10,000 or 1:5,000


Minimum mapping unit
About 0.25 ha for habitats that normally form large stands; smaller for rare or high-value stands
0.15–0.25 ha recommended for extensive types; smaller only for rarer or high-quality stands


Small and linear habitats
Springs, fens, small wetlands and caves as points or lines, with the true area or width recorded
Points and lines for occurrences under about 2,500 m² or narrower than 50 m, with true area or width recorded


Mosaics
One segment may hold several habitats, each with its share (%) and its own condition
Mosaic segments; more than five components referred to the methodologist


Boundary changes
Recorded when a boundary moves by more than about 30 m
About 30 m


Attributes per habitat
Annex I and national code; share of the segment; representativity; degradation; structure and function; typical species present; pressures; surveyor; date; photograph
Share and area per habitat; representativity, degradation, structure and function, regional context; surveyor and date per segment


Condition score
Derived from the attributes by a published lookup table, not judged afresh for each site
A quality lookup table, amended when a new combination occurs


Validation
Independent re-survey of a random 5–10 % of segments, reported as agreement on the habitat code and on the condition class
—



Czech practice follows the AOPK ČR methodology for updating the national habitat-mapping layer (Lustyk & Guth 2011). The recommended column is written for a first national map; a country mapping for the first time can hold to the same standard from the start and avoid retrofitting it.

Typical species from GBIF
Yes, to decide where to map first, but not for what is reported. The Interpretation Manual of European Union Habitats lists characteristic species for each Annex I type. Where several of them are recorded together in one 1 km cell, that cell is a candidate for early field mapping. The method works where the typical species are conspicuous and well recorded: aquatic and riparian types, and dry grasslands with their orchids and butterflies. It works poorly for forests defined by their dominant trees, and for habitats whose indicators are bryophytes or small sedges. It cannot give an area, a condition or an SDF figure. Co-occurrence is not a diagnosis either: most typical species also occur outside the habitat they characterise.
In Kosovo the plant record limits it further. Plants make up 8 % of GBIF records: 3,740 records of 938 species, of which 1,147 state an uncertainty of 100 m or better. 417 lie in Sharri National Park, which covers more than 500 km². Two or three habitat types chosen for well-recorded indicators are a fair test of the method; a national screen would mostly show where botanists have been.
Discussed in: Condition evaluation (Day 2), “A first habitat map: the minimum standard”; Field data collection (Day 3), “When the map is the working document” and “Where to start on Monday”. Karel Chobot’s habitat session (Day 1) covers monitoring design.

title: Towards Natura 2000
text:
4. Judging sufficiency without national totals
Do not wait for the denominator; make its uncertainty explicit. Estimate each national total as a range, compute the network’s share at both ends, and record a conclusion for every feature in the categories the EU’s own sufficiency process uses. Where the honest answer is that more research is needed, that process has a category for it.








Interim approach
How
Suits




The total as a range
Lower bound: the mapped or known area or population. Upper bound: modelled potential from land cover, terrain, geology and known records. Compute the network’s share against both.
Habitats with partial mapping


Occupied cells, allowing for effort
Share of occupied grid cells (the EEA 10 km grid) that fall in the network, counting only cells actually surveyed for that group
Species with scattered records


Representation across the range
Every main part of the range covered: massif, catchment, altitude belt
Every feature, whatever the data


All significant known localities
Where a feature is known from only a few sites, include every significant one
Rare and priority features


The neighbours’ figures
Article 17 estimates of neighbouring Member States and Emerald Network data of neighbouring Bern Convention Parties, as a check on plausibility
Transboundary features



The Commission’s working reference values are often quoted as a pass mark. A network holding more than 60 % of a feature’s resource is generally taken as sufficient, and one holding 20 % or less as a priority for scrutiny. They were designed as a pre-selection filter, and the current criteria say they “can never be used in isolation”. With a denominator given as a range, judge rare and priority features on the smaller of the two shares.
The conclusion codes of the EU sufficiency process are an honest way to record an interim result:







Code
Meaning




SUF
Sufficient: no further sites needed


IN MIN
Insufficient, minor: the feature should be added to the SDFs of sites already proposed


IN MOD
Insufficient, moderate: one or more further sites or extensions needed


IN MAJ
Insufficient, major: no site for the feature has been proposed yet


SR
Scientific reserve: further research needed to identify the most appropriate sites


SR Ref List
Scientific reserve on the reference list: regular occurrence still to be confirmed


CD
Correction of data: the SDF information needs correcting or completing



Keep one row per feature in a sufficiency ledger. Each row records the denominator range and its method, a data-quality code, the network’s share, the conclusion code, its date, and what evidence would change it. That last column turns every SR into a survey commission with a deadline, and makes the interim state as transparent as the final one.
Discussed in: Spatial analysis (Day 1), “A missing baseline is not a reason for inaction”. The biogeographical process itself is part of Karel Chobot’s sessions.

title: Towards Natura 2000
text:
5. Records that survive being shared
This page answers the data side of the question. Every record needs a permanent identifier, a traceable source, a version history and a validation status. Duplicates are linked, not deleted. Sensitivity is handled by generalising the public view, not by hiding the record. Ownership and the arrangement between the institutions are the subject of the joint database-architecture session (Day 1) and Martin Koška’s governance session (Day 2).







Element
Recommendation




Identifiers
A permanent UUID for every record, survey event and dataset, never re-used, with the provider’s own identifier kept alongside (Darwin Core occurrenceID). A site keeps its code through every boundary version.


Provenance
Dataset, source document, observer and method, stored as fields rather than a note.


Duplicates
Link, do not delete. Records of the same taxon, date and place from different sources share a cluster identifier; analyses count the cluster once and cite every source.


Versions
Every change to a record logged: who, when, what. Every analysis and every SDF submission made from a dated snapshot with its own DOI. Boundaries and SDFs released as numbered versions.


Validation
A status on every record, advanced in order: automated checks at import; the taxon specialist for the group; sign-off at site level; approval for SDF use.


Sensitive data
One store at full precision. The public view generalises listed sensitive species; named users under a data-use agreement see full precision, and access is logged. The sensitive list has an owner, a review cycle, and species can come off it.


Interoperability
Darwin Core for occurrences; INSPIRE Protected sites, Species distribution and Habitats and biotopes for services, through the national geoportal; one taxonomic backbone and shared code lists.



Duplication is already present in the published record. 77 groups of records, 163 records in all, describe the same species on the same day at the same place (to about 100 m) and were published in different datasets. Counted as they stand, they inflate the evidence; deleted, they lose a source. Linked, both counts are right. GBIF performs the same kind of linking across its whole index, and a national system can take its clusters as a starting point.
Discussed in: Spatial analysis (Day 1), “One central Biodiversity Information System” and “NDOP: open by default, precise by permission”.

title: Towards Natura 2000
section: 6. Bird data for Special Protection Areas
text:
6. Bird data for Special Protection Areas
Keep one table of bird records and derive the layers from it. Annex I species (Article 4(1)) and regularly occurring migratory species (Article 4(2)) belong in attributes, not in separate datasets that drift apart. To move from IBA, KBA and occurrence data to an SPA proposal, each species that is to qualify the site needs three things. It needs a current population estimate from standardised counts, and a stated criterion that estimate meets. It also needs a boundary drawn around the habitat the population actually uses.








Field
Content
Why




Annex I
Yes or no, from the consolidated Directive
The Article 4(1) trigger


Regular migrant
Yes or no, from a national list the Ministry adopts and versions
The Article 4(2) trigger; the list is a decision, not a lookup


Population type
p permanent, r reproducing, c concentration, w wintering: the SDF codes
One species can need different sites in different seasons


Breeding evidence
Possible, probable or confirmed, as in the European breeding bird atlas
A record in the breeding season is not a breeding record


Count and unit
A number, with its unit: pairs, individuals, males, calling males
Only counts with units can be summed or set against a threshold


Method and effort
Protocol, duration, distance, whether all species were reported
Turns a record into a survey, and makes absence usable



The working layers are views over that one table: Annex I breeding, Annex I passage and wintering, regular migrants, and congregations. When a record is corrected, every layer follows.
What an SPA proposal needs, beyond the IBA:

The IBA inventory is the starting point. The Court of Justice has treated it as the best available scientific reference for judging whether enough SPAs have been classified (Case C-3/96, Commission v Netherlands). An IBA is still not an SPA proposal: its boundary is often coarse, and some of its qualifying species cannot trigger an SPA at all (see below).
A population estimate for each trigger species, given as minimum and maximum with a unit, a year and an SDF data-quality code. It should come from standardised surveys over at least two or three seasons:

territory mapping or point counts for breeding birds;
nest surveys for raptors;
International Waterbird Census counts for wintering waterbirds;
standardised counts at passage bottlenecks.

The criterion it meets. BirdLife’s EU-level criteria are tested definitions: C2, the site regularly holds at least 1 % of a flyway or EU population of a species threatened in the EU; C6, the site is one of the five most important in its region for such a species.
A boundary around what the birds use: nesting, feeding and roosting areas, including the fields or river they commute to. Check it against the IBA outline; do not copy it.
eBird’s own dataset for analysis. Request the eBird Basic Dataset from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology. It carries the effort fields and whether each checklist reports every species detected, which turns a checklist’s missing species into non-detections. The copy on GBIF is presence-only.

title: NaturAL project, Albania: small terrestrial mammals
text:
What it is
NaturAL, “Strengthening capacity in National Nature Protection – preparation for Natura 2000 network”, was Albania’s project to prepare its Natura 2000 network. One of its published outputs is a data paper in ZooKeys (Bego, Saçdanaku, Pacifici & Rondinini 2018) on the distribution and diversity of Albania’s small terrestrial mammals. It reports 31 species from field campaigns in the summers and autumns of 2016 and 2017 in priority protected areas, and it is licensed CC BY 4.0.
The paper is relevant here because of where the fieldwork took place. It covers Kukës district (Novosejë-Shishtavec and Korab-Koritnik), Tropojë, Has (Krumë and Pashtrik) and the Albanian Alps: the Albanian side of the Sharr, Pashtrik and Bjeshkët e Nemuna/Prokletije massifs that Kosovo shares.

section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
Most small mammals on the Habitats Directive annexes are not among the species here. The value is as a reference list for the same mountains: which shrews, voles and mice a systematic survey found a few kilometres across the border, against which the patchy Kosovo record can be judged. It also shows what a Natura 2000 preparation project in a neighbour chose to survey and publish, which is a model for Kosovo’s own. Tier: to be set once the locality precision is read (tiers).

title: Article 17 reporting under the Habitats Directive, 2013–2018
text:
What it is
Every six years each EU Member State reports, under Article 17 of the Habitats Directive, on the conservation status of the habitat types and species listed in the Directive’s annexes. The European Environment Agency (EEA) publishes the reports as two linked products: tabular assessments of status and trend for each country and biogeographical region, and a spatial layer in which each country maps where every habitat and species occurs on the 10 km ETRS89 grid. The public version for the 2013–2018 round was released in August 2020, for the EU of 28 countries, and is licensed CC-BY 4.0 to the EEA and the Commission’s Directorate-General for Environment.
The EEA describes the spatial part as habitat and species distribution data in 10 km grid cells “as reported by Member States”. That wording matters here: the maps are what each country chose to report, compiled rather than harmonised, and a country boundary is also the edge of the data.

title: Article 17 reporting under the Habitats Directive, 2013–2018
text:
Access
The dataset is open and needs no account. The GeoPackage is 151,576,576 bytes (about 145 MB), so it is not copied into this repository: GDAL reads it over HTTP range requests (/vsicurl/) and fetches only the pages that cover a box around Kosovo, as the pipeline already does for the protected-area inventory. The result, about a thousand distribution features, is cut to the 10 km cells within 100 km of Kosovo and cached as a small GeoPackage.

Show how the border-zone extract is built
# Runs only when the cache is missing. Any failure is caught and reported below.
build_error <- NULL
if (!file.exists(cache)) {
  build_error <- tryCatch({
    Sys.setenv(GDAL_DISABLE_READDIR_ON_OPEN = "EMPTY_DIR",
               CPL_VSIL_CURL_CHUNK_SIZE = "1048576",
               CPL_VSIL_CURL_CACHE_SIZE = "524288000")
    src <- paste0("/vsicurl/", share)
    ko   <- st_transform(st_union(kosovo_outline()), 3035)
    zone <- st_buffer(ko, 100000)
    box  <- st_as_text(st_as_sfc(st_bbox(zone)))

    sp <- st_read(src, layer = "Art17_species_distribution_2013_2018_MS",
                  wkt_filter = box, quiet = TRUE)
    hb <- st_read(src, layer = "Art17_habitats_distribution_2013_2018_MS",
                  wkt_filter = box, quiet = TRUE)
    sp_names <- unique(st_read(src, layer = "speciesMSassessment",
                               quiet = TRUE)[, c("speciescode", "speciesname")])

    # Each feature is one species (or habitat) in one country and region, its
    # 10 km cells dissolved into one shape. The cells are rebuilt from the EEA
    # grid, whose corners sit on round 10 km multiples of EPSG:3035.
    bb <- st_bbox(zone)
    bb[c("xmin", "ymin")] <- floor(bb[c("xmin", "ymin")] / 1e4) * 1e4
    bb[c("xmax", "ymax")] <- ceiling(bb[c("xmax", "ymax")] / 1e4) * 1e4
    grid <- st_sf(geometry = st_make_grid(st_as_sfc(bb), cellsize = 1e4))
    grid <- grid[lengths(st_intersects(grid, zone)) > 0, ]
    grid$cell_id <- sprintf("10kmE%dN%d",
      floor(st_coordinates(st_centroid(grid))[, 1] / 1e4),
      floor(st_coordinates(st_centroid(grid))[, 2] / 1e4))
    grid$dist_km <- round(as.numeric(st_distance(grid, ko)) / 1000, 1)

    centres <- st_centroid(st_geometry(grid))
    explode <- function(x, code_col, kind) {
      hit <- st_intersects(centres, x)
      do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(hit), function(i) {
        if (!length(hit[[i]])) return(NULL)
        f <- st_drop_geometry(x)[hit[[i]], ]
        data.frame(cell_id = grid$cell_id[i], kind = kind,
                   code = as.character(f[[code_col]]), country = f$country,
                   region = f$region,
                   sensitive = if ("sensitive" %in% names(f)) f$sensitive
                               else NA_character_)
      }))
    }
    long <- rbind(explode(sp, "speciescode", "species"),
                  explode(hb, "habitatcode", "habitat"))
    long$name <- sp_names$speciesname[match(long$code, sp_names$speciescode)]
    long$name[long$kind == "habitat"] <- NA

    grid <- grid[grid$cell_id %in% long$cell_id, ]
    st_write(grid, cache, layer = "cells", delete_dsn = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)
    st_write(long, cache, layer = "features", append = FALSE, quiet = TRUE)
    NULL
  }, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
}
have_cache <- file.exists(cache)

title: Article 17 reporting under the Habitats Directive, 2013–2018
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
It answers a question none of the report’s current sources can: which Annex I habitats and Annex II species the EU’s own reporting places closest to Kosovo. The assessment tables in the same file add each feature’s status in the reporting country and region, joined on CO_MS_RE. That is a starting list for the sufficiency ledger and a plausibility check for the directive-listed species the GBIF extract finds. At 10 km it serves the national screening tier only.

title: Article 17 reporting under the Habitats Directive, 2013–2018
text:
Caveats and sensitivity

The countries that surround Kosovo (Serbia, Montenegro, Albania, North Macedonia) are outside the EU and absent, so the nearest data lie about 50 km away, and most lie beyond it.
The public version leaves out sensitive species altogether: the EEA’s README describes it as “the public dataset, without sensitive species”. A persecuted raptor or a collected orchid can therefore be missing from these lists even where a neighbour reported it. The extract keeps the sensitive column the file carries.
The data are ten years old by the end of the next round; see the open check below on 2019–2024.

title: Article 17 reporting under the Habitats Directive, 2013–2018
text:
Integration into the pipeline
Low effort. The remote read above is the same pattern as kosovo_protected_areas(). A proposed art17_border_features(boundary, radius_km = c(50, 100)) in R/functions.R, called from a new section after 7b of pipeline.R, would write the long table to data/ for the report to read. This page does not change pipeline.R.

Citation
Neither the catalogue record nor the README gives a citation string. The CC-BY 4.0 licence requires attribution to the copyright holders it names, the Commission’s DG Environment and the EEA, so the dataset is cited here by its own title: Conservation status of habitat types and species: datasets from Article 17, Habitats Directive 92/43/EEC reporting (2013–2018), public version, August 2020. European Environment Agency and European Commission DG Environment, CC-BY 4.0. Catalogue record 9f71b3e3-f8ec-442b-a2d5-c3c190605ac4.

title: Biodiversiteti i Kosovës
text:
What it is
Biodiversiteti i Kosovës (“Kosovo’s biodiversity”) is a 22-page overview in Albanian, prepared by Qenan Maxhuni, biodiversity officer at KEPA and the Kosovo Institute for Nature Protection. The PDF dates from July 2012. It describes the country’s flora, vegetation, fauna and main natural areas and names the Sharr mountains and Bjeshkët e Nemuna as the richest in plants and animals. Its Table 7 gives approximate species numbers per group, many marked as likely underestimates: about 1,800 flowering plants, 180 birds, 45 mammals, 14 amphibians, 14 reptiles and 30 freshwater fish. It states plainly that Kosovo does not yet have a complete inventory of its biodiversity, and, at the time, that it had no red list.

title: Copernicus Digital Elevation Model
text:
What it is
The Copernicus DEM is a digital surface model: as its AWS readme puts it, it represents the surface of the Earth “including buildings, infrastructure and vegetation”. It comes in two public instances, GLO-30 at 30 m, not yet released everywhere, and GLO-90 at 90 m, with worldwide coverage. The copy on Amazon’s open-data registry is cut into 1° tiles as cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs and is free for the general public under the Copernicus DEM licence.

Kosovo spans six GLO-90 tiles. Because the files are cloud-optimised, GDAL reads only the blocks it needs, and the crop is cached here. The six tiles are combined into one virtual mosaic (terra::vrt()) before cropping, so the code does not need to know which tile holds which part of the country; the tile names follow a fixed pattern of latitude and longitude, which the helper tile_url() above writes out.


Show the remote crop
build_error <- NULL
if (!file.exists(cache)) {
  build_error <- tryCatch({
    Sys.setenv(GDAL_DISABLE_READDIR_ON_OPEN = "EMPTY_DIR")
    tiles <- expand.grid(lat = 41:43, lon = 20:21)
    r  <- vrt(paste0("/vsicurl/", mapply(tile_url, tiles$lat, tiles$lon)))
    ko <- vect(kosovo_outline())
    k  <- round(mask(crop(r, ko, snap = "out"), ko))
    writeRaster(k, cache, overwrite = TRUE, datatype = "INT2S",
                gdal = "COMPRESS=DEFLATE")
    NULL
  }, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
}
have_cache <- file.exists(cache)

title: Copernicus Digital Elevation Model
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
Elevation separates habitats the land-cover data cannot: alpine grassland from lowland grassland, subalpine beech from thermophilous oak. The altitude belts above give the representation test of question 4 (“every altitude belt covered”) its denominator, and a terrain model is one of the layers the boundary workflow of question 2 draws along (watersheds, ridges). GLO-90 serves the national tier; GLO-30, if available, would come closer to site work.

title: Copernicus Digital Elevation Model
text:
Caveats and sensitivity

A surface model: in forest it measures the canopy, not the ground.
At 90 m, narrow gorges and ridges are smoothed.
No sensitive content.

title: Copernicus Digital Elevation Model
text:
Integration into the pipeline
Low effort. A proposed kosovo_dem(boundary) in R/functions.R would do the crop above and cache data/kosovo_dem_glo90.tif; the habitat screen could then split its classes by altitude belt, much as it splits them by biogeographical region today. pipeline.R is not changed.

The second European Breeding Bird Atlas, published in 2020 by the European Bird Census Council (EBCC) with Lynx Edicions, maps the distribution, abundance and change of Europe’s breeding birds from fieldwork carried out mostly between 2013 and 2017 by some 120,000 fieldworkers in 48 countries. title: European Breeding Bird Atlas 2
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
Nine in ten of the 28,785 bird records in the report’s GBIF extract come from eBird checklists, and they cluster where observers go. An atlas is a systematic survey with breeding evidence in every square, which is what an SPA case needs to separate breeding from passage birds (see question 6). The 10 km modelled maps would also give a first, consistent distribution for Annex I species. At 50 km and 10 km the data serve the national screening tier.

text:

Access terms are unconfirmed; the claim of freely licensed 50 km data from the desk review could not be verified.
Modelled 10 km maps are predictions, not observations.
Atlas data must be shown at their native grid; finer locations for sensitive species must not be derived from them.

title: European Commission Kosovo Report 2025
text:
What it is
Each year the European Commission assesses Kosovo’s progress towards the EU across the chapters of the acquis. The 2025 report was published on 4 November 2025. Its Chapter 27, on environment and climate change, finds Kosovo “at an early stage of preparation” with limited progress.
On nature protection the report is short and specific. Kosovo made limited progress. The identification of potential Natura 2000 sites “is at a very early stage”. Protected areas lack appropriate management and suffer from pollution, illegal activities and weak enforcement. There was no progress in aligning legislation on nature protection. The adoption of a strategy for environmental protection and sustainable development for 2024–2033 remains pending. On forests it notes that 40 per cent of public forests are subject to uncontrolled or illegal harvesting.

title: Ecosystem types of Europe 2012, version 3.1
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
The report’s habitat screen reads CORINE Land Cover through a crosswalk to Annex I. This map is the EEA’s own step from land cover towards habitats, at the same 100 m, done once for all of Europe. It offers an independent second opinion on where grasslands, heaths, forests and mires lie, and it is consistent with the maps neighbouring countries would use. At EUNIS level 2 it does not name Annex I types, and it serves the national screening tier only.

title: Ecosystem types of Europe 2012, version 3.1
text:
Caveats and sensitivity

It describes 2012 and is built on CORINE Land Cover of that period.
Level-2 classes are broad: “Broadleaved deciduous woodland” (G1) spans most of Kosovo’s Annex I forest types, and forest that qualifies as none.
The EEA estimates its reliability in a separate map that this page has not yet read.
No species locations; nothing sensitive.

title: Emerald Network
text:
What it is
The Emerald Network is the Bern Convention’s counterpart of Natura 2000: a network of Areas of Special Conservation Interest (ASCIs) that the Convention’s non-EU Parties propose, have assessed, and adopt. The data are owned by the Council of Europe and processed and published by the EEA. The 2025 version, published on 19 May 2026 under CC-BY 4.0, reflects the submissions the Standing Committee adopted in December 2025.
Kosovo is not a Party. Its own biodiversity action plan says so plainly: “Kosovo is not a Party to the Bern Convention, meaning that the Emerald Network has not been developed in the country” (MESP, Action Plan for Biodiversity 2016–2020). The desk review therefore expected this page to be “Not applicable to Kosovo”. The check below shows why that is not quite right.

Show how the sites around Kosovo are fetched
build_error <- NULL
if (!file.exists(cache)) {
  build_error <- tryCatch({
    source("../R/functions.R", local = TRUE)
    ko   <- st_transform(st_union(kosovo_outline()), 3035)
    zone <- st_buffer(ko, 50000)
    sites <- arcgis_query_sf(service, st_bbox(st_transform(zone, 4326)),
                             fields = "SITECODE,SITENAME,COUNTRY_CODE,SITESTATUS,AREAHA,DATE_PROP_ASCI",
                             verbose = FALSE)
    sites <- st_make_valid(sites)
    sites <- sites[lengths(st_intersects(sites, zone)) > 0, ]
    sites$site_ha <- as.numeric(st_area(sites)) / 1e4
    sites$ha_in_kosovo <- as.numeric(vapply(seq_len(nrow(sites)), function(i)
      sum(as.numeric(st_area(st_intersection(st_geometry(sites)[i], ko)))), 0)) / 1e4
    sites$km_to_kosovo <- round(as.numeric(st_distance(sites, ko)) / 1000, 1)
    sites$proposed <- format(as.POSIXct(sites$DATE_PROP_ASCI / 1000,
                                        origin = "1970-01-01", tz = "UTC"), "%Y")
    st_write(st_intersection(sites, zone), cache, delete_dsn = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)
    NULL
  }, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
}

33 Emerald sites lie within 50 km of Kosovo (AL 4, ME 10, MK 6, RS 13). 5 Serbian candidate sites, coded RS, reach inside Kosovo and cover 230,393 ha of it, about 21 per cent of the country. Another 5 sites of Montenegro, Albania and North Macedonia overlap the border by 2,045 ha in all; at a scale of 1:100,000 much of that is the difference between the Emerald outlines and the OpenStreetMap border. No site carries a Kosovo code (XK, XKX, KOS or KV).
The Serbian sites were proposed in 2006, before Kosovo’s declaration of independence, and the Emerald data still file them under Serbia. Mirusha and Gërmia are named after places in Kosovo and lie inside it; the Kosovo parts of Prokletije and Šar Planina take in the western and southern mountains where both national parks lie. This is the “Kosovo merged into RS” pattern: a user who filters the Emerald data by country counts Kosovo ground as Serbian without knowing it, and any statistic computed per country, sufficiency included, may do the same.

title: Emerald Network
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
Two things. First, the neighbours’ candidate sites along the border, which a Kosovo proposal should meet rather than stop short of. Second, a warning for every European dataset used in this section: Kosovo’s territory can be present under another country’s code, and a check by code alone would miss it. Emerald boundaries are drawn at 1:100,000, so they serve the site tier only as a first outline (tiers). The Emerald Standard Data Form is structurally close to the Natura 2000 SDF, and its guidance is worth reading when Kosovo designs its own forms; that reading is an open action, since coe.int was blocked.

title: Emerald Network
text:
Caveats and sensitivity

Candidate status is the first of the Emerald stages; none of these border sites is adopted.
The Serbian sites inside Kosovo date from 2006–2008 and describe data of that time.
The status of those sites under the Convention could not be checked, because coe.int was unreachable.

title: Conservation assessment of the endemic plants from Kosovo (Hacquetia, 2017)
text:
What it is
Millaku, Krasniqi, Berisha and Rexhepi assessed the conservation status of 16 plant taxa endemic to Kosovo or the Balkans against the IUCN Red List categories and criteria (guidelines version 8.1). The paper appeared in Hacquetia 16(1) in 2017 under a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 licence. Of the 16 taxa, four are Balkan endemics, eight local endemics and four stenoendemics. Six grow only on serpentine, five on limestone, four on carbonate substrates and one on silicate. The most threatened, Solenanthus krasniqii, was reduced to about 20 mature individuals.

title: Conservation assessment of the endemic plants from Kosovo (Hacquetia, 2017)
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
Endemic plants of serpentine and limestone mark exactly the habitats, such as serpentine grasslands and rocky slopes, that a Kosovo site list would need to cover. Several may not be on Annex II, but a national assessment of their status is evidence for choosing between candidate sites that hold the same Annex I habitat. It serves the national tier; with localities, it could inform site boundaries.

title: Conservation assessment of the endemic plants from Kosovo (Hacquetia, 2017)
text:
Caveats and sensitivity

Sixteen taxa is a small, focused set, not a flora-wide list; the Red Book of Vascular Flora (2013) covers 237.
National assessments made in 2017 may be out of date.
Stenoendemics with a few dozen individuals are at risk from collecting and must never be mapped precisely in public.

title: EUNIS habitat maps at level 3 (Si-Moussi et al. 2025)
text:
What it is
Si-Moussi and colleagues trained ensemble machine-learning models on vegetation plots from the European Vegetation Archive (1990–2021), satellite imagery and climatic, topographic and soil predictors, and predicted the most probable EUNIS habitat at level 3 for every 100 m cell of the EEA39 countries. The data paper, in Scientific Data (11 December 2025), defines that study area explicitly to include Kosovo with the other Western Balkan countries. The maps are on Zenodo under CC-BY 4.0: a “wall-to-wall” map of the most likely current habitat, filtered by CORINE Land Cover 2018, plus probability and top-three maps per habitat group.

title: EUNIS habitat maps at level 3 (Si-Moussi et al. 2025)
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
Kosovo has no Annex I habitat map, and this is the closest thing to one that exists: a level-3 prediction that separates, for instance, beech forest from oak forest, and dry from mesic grassland. Through the crosswalk it gives a first, clearly provisional list of where to look for which Annex I types, which is exactly the input the mapping standard in question 3 asks for before fieldwork. It complements the report’s CORINE screen by predicting habitats from climate, terrain and soils as well as land cover. At 100 m and as a model it serves the national screening tier only.

title: EUNIS habitat maps at level 3 (Si-Moussi et al. 2025)
text:
Caveats and sensitivity

It is a model. Its accuracy in the Balkans depends on how many training plots lay there, which this page has not yet checked.
Only the most likely class is used; the confidence layers are not yet read.
Some classes are implausible at face value: “Large-scale ornamental garden area” (V21) is predicted over about 13 per cent of Kosovo. That says more about how the land-cover filter treats Kosovo’s mixed farmland and settlements than about gardens, and it is a reason to read the class list critically rather than as an inventory.
The Annex I crosswalk is European, many-to-many and indicative. Several candidate types it lists are not Balkan habitats at all.
No species locations; nothing sensitive.

title: EUNIS habitat maps at level 3 (Si-Moussi et al. 2025)
text:
Integration into the pipeline
Medium effort. A proposed kosovo_eunis_habitats(boundary) in R/functions.R would do the crop above; the crosswalk would live in an editable CSV beside data/crosswalk_clc_annex1.csv, reviewed by a specialist, so the report could show where the CORINE and EUNIS screens agree. The package eunis.habitats would become a pipeline dependency. pipeline.R is not changed here.

title: European Red Lists
text:
What it is
The European Red Lists assess the extinction risk of more than 10,000 European species, from mammals and birds to bees, grasshoppers and ferns, under the IUCN guidelines for regional assessment, at two levels: the EU and pan-Europe. The EEA publishes the results as tables on its datahub; the current series covers assessments from 2009 to 2022, and the dataset’s owner is the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Environment.
For Kosovo, the pan-European level is the relevant one, and whether its assessments count Kosovo as a country of occurrence is the open question. A related finding bears on it. The 2024 Scientific Data database of European national red lists for vascular plants (Lončarević et al.) treats Kosovo as a country with a red list of its own. Its authors removed the Kosovo taxa from Serbia’s red book of 1999, and did not add them to the Kosovo list.

title: European Red Lists
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
The report already carries each species’ global IUCN category. A European category is often more telling for Natura 2000: a species of Least Concern globally can be threatened in Europe, and the Habitats Directive is a European instrument. Where the assessments list countries of occurrence, they also give a European view of which species occur in Kosovo. It serves the national tier.

title: European Red Lists

European and EU27 categories differ; the report should say which it uses.

title: Global Forest Change (Hansen et al.)
text:
What it is
Hansen and colleagues at the University of Maryland map, for every 30 m pixel of the world’s land, the tree cover in 2000 and the year in which any stand-replacing loss of it was detected. The data behind their 2013 paper in Science have been extended every year since. Version 1.13, covering 2000–2025, is the latest on the download page and replaces version 1.12 (2000–2024); both are licensed CC BY 4.0. The desk review named the product without a version; v1.13 is the one used here.

title: Global Forest Change (Hansen et al.)
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
Forest habitat types will make up much of a Kosovo network, and the European Commission’s 2025 report says that 40 per cent of public forests are subject to uncontrolled or illegal harvesting. Loss mapped year by year shows where that pressure lands, whether inside existing protected areas, and whether it is increasing. That is evidence for the pressures section of an SDF and for the trend in a forest habitat’s area. At 30 m it serves the national tier, and the site tier as a first screen.

title: Global Forest Change (Hansen et al.)
text:
Caveats and sensitivity

“Loss” is stand-replacing removal of tree cover; it includes legal harvesting, fire and windthrow, and cannot tell them apart.
Read the usage notes on the download page before comparing early years with late ones; this check reports the years as the layer gives them.
No species locations; nothing sensitive.

title: Global Forest Change (Hansen et al.)
text:
Integration into the pipeline
Low effort. A proposed kosovo_forest_loss(boundary) in R/functions.R would do the crop above; the report could add loss per protected area and per municipality beside its habitat screen. pipeline.R is not changed.

title: Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas and Key Biodiversity Areas
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
The IBA inventory is the starting reference for SPAs; the Court of Justice has treated it as the best available scientific evidence for judging whether enough SPAs are classified (see question 6). With boundaries, the report could say how much of Šar and Prokletije’s IBAs lie in Kosovo, and draw candidate SPAs against them. Boundaries serve the site tier as a first outline; the attributes serve national screening.

title: Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas and Key Biodiversity Areas
text:
Caveats and sensitivity

Centroids say where a site is, not how much of it lies on either side of a border.
The qualifying populations date from 1998 to 2017 (see the report’s table), several of them old.
Boundaries are released under terms that come with the request; they must not be scraped from the map server.

What it is
Important Plant Areas (IPAs) are sites identified, under a programme run by Plantlife, as the most important places for wild plants and their habitats. That phrase suggests the Serbian inventory may reach into Kosovo, as the Serbian Emerald candidate sites do (see Emerald Network); it does not confirm any IPA there. section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
The Habitats Directive’s plant side, Annex I habitats and Annex II plants, is where Kosovo’s data are thinnest. IPAs are expert judgements of where plant importance concentrates. A Kosovo IPA list, if one exists, would be an obvious shortlist to test against candidate SCIs.
The Serbian page raises the same question as the Emerald Network and IBA pages: whether a regional inventory compiled with Serbia counts Kosovo’s mountains as Serbian sites. If it does, those IPAs are Kosovo evidence filed under another country, and they should be found and read, not dismissed as foreign.

title: Occurrence data papers from Kosovo (Biodiversity Data Journal)
text:
What it is
Kosovo’s biodiversity is being described paper by paper. The Biodiversity Data Journal (BDJ), published by Pensoft, is one of the main venues: its articles are open under CC BY 4.0, and Pensoft publishes each article’s occurrence records to GBIF as a dataset of its own. The desk review’s example, Krasniqi & Berisha (2025), records Anchusella cretica for the first time in Kosovo, a new genus and species for the national flora, from four populations found in 2024–2025 and assessed as Near Threatened nationally. Most of the other Kosovo papers in BDJ describe caddisflies, including species new to science from Kosovo’s mountain rivers.
The question for this page is not whether the papers exist but whether their records are already in the GBIF extract the report is built on.

text:
Kosovo coverage check
For every BDJ paper with Kosovo in its title, the check looks up GBIF’s dataset for the article’s DOI, counts its records inside Kosovo (GADM XKO), notes the country codes they carry, and tests whether the dataset is among those in the report’s download.


Show the check
if (!file.exists(cache)) {
  res <- tryCatch({
    papers <- jsonlite::fromJSON(paste0(
      "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=",
      "JOURNAL:%22Biodiversity%20Data%20Journal%22%20AND%20TITLE:Kosovo",
      "&format=json&pageSize=100"))$resultList$result
    reg <- read.csv(file.path(sources_root(), "data", "dataset_registry.csv"))
    do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(papers)), function(i) {
      doi <- papers$doi[i]
      ds  <- jsonlite::fromJSON(paste0("https://api.gbif.org/v1/dataset/doi/", doi))$results
      key <- if (length(ds) && NROW(ds)) ds$key[1] else NA
      occ <- if (is.na(key)) NULL else jsonlite::fromJSON(sprintf(
        "https://api.gbif.org/v1/occurrence/search?datasetKey=%s&limit=300&facet=country", key))
      codes <- if (is.null(occ) || !length(occ$facets$counts)) "" else
        paste(occ$facets$counts[[1]]$name, collapse = ", ")
      u <- if (is.null(occ)) NULL else occ$results$coordinateUncertaintyInMeters
      unc <- if (is.null(u) || all(is.na(u))) NA_real_ else stats::median(u, na.rm = TRUE)
      xko <- if (is.na(key)) NA else jsonlite::fromJSON(sprintf(
        "https://api.gbif.org/v1/occurrence/search?datasetKey=%s&gadmGid=XKO&limit=0", key))$count
      data.frame(year = papers$pubYear[i], doi = doi,
                 title = trimws(gsub("[[:space:]]+", " ", gsub("<[^>]+>|<[^&]*>", " ",
                                                         papers$title[i]))),
                 gbif_dataset = key, records_total = if (is.null(occ)) NA else occ$count,
                 records_in_kosovo = xko, country_codes = codes,
                 median_uncertainty_m = unc,
                 in_report_download = !is.na(key) & key %in% reg$datasetKey)
    }))
  }, error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.null(res)) write.csv(res, cache, row.names = FALSE)
}

title: Occurrence data papers from Kosovo (Biodiversity Data Journal)
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
New national records and newly described species are exactly the features a Natura 2000 gap analysis must not miss, and they are usually known from a single site. Knowing which of them are already in GBIF, and so in the report, tells the reader whether the report’s species lists are current. None of the paper datasets states a coordinate uncertainty, so by the report’s rules they sit at the national screening tier until someone checks each locality against the paper; a verified locality could then reach the delineation tier.

title: Occurrence data papers from Kosovo (Biodiversity Data Journal)
text:
Caveats and sensitivity

The search covers BDJ titles containing “Kosovo” only; papers that name a mountain or river instead are missed.
A dataset on GBIF is not necessarily in the report’s download: the download is a dated snapshot.
Newly described species with one known site are vulnerable to collecting; check before mapping them publicly.

title: Occurrence data papers from Kosovo (Biodiversity Data Journal)
text:
Integration into the pipeline
Low effort: the records already reach GBIF. What the pipeline lacks is a refresh. Re-running the download (a new DOI) picks them up, and a proposed check_recent_datasets(since = download_date) could list GBIF datasets with Kosovo records created after the snapshot, so the report can say what it does not yet include. pipeline.R is not changed.

title: Natura 2000 research in Montenegro: species reports
text:
What it is
Montenegro is preparing its Natura 2000 network ahead of accession. On 25 March 2026 its Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) reported two days of expert meetings to finalise the first draft proposal of Natura 2000 areas. The work brought together the EPA, the EU IPA project “Support for the establishment of the Natura 2000 network for Montenegro”, run by Eptisa, and experts who had carried out eight years of field research mapping habitats and species. The EPA describes Natura 2000 as “one of the key requirements” of Montenegro’s accession, and part of the closing benchmark for Chapter 27.
The “species reports” named in the desk review come from that research. The only copies found are uploads by individuals on academia.edu and ResearchGate. Neither could be opened, so their content is not described here.

What it is
Two sources, one of them governmental, confirm that a first identification of potential Natura 2000 sites in Kosovo was made more than fifteen years ago. title: Emerald Network sufficiency in neighbouring countries
text:
What it is
Under the Bern Convention each Party proposes Emerald sites, and regional biogeographical seminars then judge, species by species and habitat by habitat, whether a country’s list is sufficient. The share of features found sufficient is reported as a sufficiency index. For Kosovo’s neighbours the index says how complete their networks are along the shared mountains, and therefore how much of a transboundary network already exists on the other side of the border.
The figures below come from a secondary source only. CEE Bankwatch Network reported on 9 December 2024, after the 44th meeting of the Convention’s Standing Committee, that all Western Balkan countries must reach a 35 per cent sufficiency target by 2030, and gave each country’s current index. The primary Council of Europe documents could not be opened.

title: Emerald Network sufficiency in neighbouring countries
text:
Kosovo coverage check
The sufficiency index is a national figure and says nothing about Kosovo directly. What can be checked is what each neighbour has put on the ground near Kosovo.


Show how the neighbours’ sites near Kosovo are counted
build_error <- NULL
if (!file.exists(cache)) {
  build_error <- tryCatch({
    source("../R/functions.R", local = TRUE)
    ko   <- st_transform(st_union(kosovo_outline()), 3035)
    zone <- st_buffer(ko, 50000)
    s <- arcgis_query_sf(service, st_bbox(st_transform(zone, 4326)),
                         fields = "SITECODE,SITENAME,COUNTRY_CODE,SITESTATUS",
                         verbose = FALSE) |> st_make_valid()
    s <- s[lengths(st_intersects(s, zone)) > 0, ]
    ring <- st_difference(zone, ko)
    s$ha_in_ring <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(s)), function(i)
      sum(as.numeric(st_area(st_intersection(st_geometry(s)[i], ring)))), 0) / 1e4
    write.csv(st_drop_geometry(s), cache, row.names = FALSE)
    NULL
  }, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
}

section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
It sets expectations. If the neighbours have proved between 13 and 28 per cent of their features sufficient, as the secondary source reports, a Kosovo network will be judged in a region where few boundaries are settled. It also flags a practical risk: the Serbian candidate sites inside Kosovo (see Emerald Network) may enter Serbia’s statistics, and a Kosovo sufficiency ledger (question 4) should not count the same ground twice.

Caveats and sensitivity

The four percentages are secondary. Until the Council of Europe document is read, treat them as reported, not verified.
Sufficiency is judged per biogeographical region; a single national figure hides regional differences.
The index is a share of features, not of territory.

title: Protected and strictly protected wild species (AI 18/2012 and its successors)
text:
What it is
Under the Law on Nature Protection (No. 03/L-233), the ministry responsible for the environment declares by administrative instruction which wild species are protected and which strictly protected. The desk review named Administrative Instruction No. 18/2012, which the Red Book of Vascular Flora (2013) also cites as one basis for its selection. It is not the current act. The Official Gazette holds Administrative Instruction MEA No. 12/2020 “for the declaration of protected and strictly protected wild species”, published on 29 December 2020, which supersedes Administrative Instruction No. 12/2017 on strictly protected wild species. Whether 12/2017 in turn repealed 18/2012 was not confirmed.

title: Red Book of Fauna of the Republic of Kosovo
text:
What it is
Libri i Kuq i Faunës së Republikës së Kosovës is Kosovo’s red book of animals. It was published in Prishtinë in 2018 by the Ministry of Environment and Spatial Planning, with the Kosovo Environmental Protection Agency (KEPA) and the Kosovo Institute for Nature Protection, edited by Halil Ibrahimi with nine co-authors from Kosovo and the region. The desk review cited it as Ibrahimi et al. 2019, which matches the PDF’s date of July 2019 rather than the imprint year of 2018. It runs to 203 pages in Albanian, with chapters by group (molluscs, oligochaetes, insects, fish, reptiles, birds and others), national IUCN categories, and a species account for each listed animal. Those accounts name the localities where each species is known in Kosovo and carry distribution maps.

Kosovo coverage check
The book is national by definition. The check that matters is whether its locality data exist as data. The desk review’s note that “locality data are not published” holds, with that nuance.

title: Red Book of Fauna of the Republic of Kosovo
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
A national red list says which animals are at risk in Kosovo itself, which neither the EU annexes nor the global IUCN list (both already in the report) can. Species that are nationally threatened and also on Annex II are obvious priorities for site selection; species threatened nationally but absent from the annexes point to where national protection must do what Natura 2000 will not. It serves the national tier.

title: Red Book of Fauna of the Republic of Kosovo
text:
Caveats and sensitivity

All rights reserved; the book can be cited and read, not republished.
Maps and named localities of threatened species are sensitive. Any use in this site must stay at 10 km or coarser for persecuted or collected species and state what was generalised.
Categories follow IUCN regional guidelines as applied by the authors; they are not comparable one-to-one with global categories.

title: Red Book of Fauna of the Republic of Kosovo

Medium effort. A proposed data/kosovo_red_list_fauna.csv, holding species, national category and GBIF key only, built by an R/build_red_list.R like the existing R/build_directive_list.R, would let pipeline.R add a nationalRedList column to every record. That needs either the Ministry’s agreement or a table it publishes. pipeline.R is not changed here.

text:
What it is
The desk review grouped soils and geology under one lead. The soil half has an obvious open source: SoilGrids, ISRIC’s global maps of soil properties at 250 m, served as cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs behind VRT files at files.isric.org. title: Soil and geology layers (SoilGrids and others)
text:
Kosovo coverage check
Inside Kosovo: 174,600 cells of 250 m, 3248 of them no-data (1.9 per cent). Soil organic carbon in the top 5 cm ranges from 298 to 1,697 in the layer’s stored units (dg/kg per the SoilGrids convention, to be confirmed on isric.org). No country attribute, so no country code applies.






SoilGrids is stored in the Interrupted Goode Homolosine projection, an equal-area projection for the whole globe, unlike every other layer in this section. The build step therefore projects the Kosovo outline into the raster’s projection and crops there, rather than reprojecting the raster to fit the outline: reprojecting a raster resamples every cell, and doing it before cropping would mean resampling far more of the globe than is needed. Only the map on this page reprojects, to Web Mercator for display.






WarningTo be completed



Geology: no open layer was checked. Find one, crop it to Kosovo, and report the area of serpentine and limestone, which are the substrates Kosovo’s endemic plants depend on.

title: Soil and geology layers (SoilGrids and others)
section: What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
text:
What it adds for Natura 2000 in Kosovo
Soil and substrate are covariates for habitat models, and substrate in particular separates Annex I types that land cover cannot: calcareous from siliceous grassland and rock, serpentine grassland from both. SoilGrids gives consistent soil properties; a geological map would give the substrate. National screening only (tier). Of the two halves, the missing geology matters more for Kosovo: a serpentine outcrop is a candidate site for its endemic flora whatever its soil carbon, and no layer checked so far can show one.

SoilGrids is a global model; local accuracy in Kosovo’s mountains is unknown.
The geology half of this page is unverified.
